title: SYSTEM OF STATE GOVERNANCE MECHANISMS FOR THE DEVELOPMENT OF INNOVATIVE ENTREPRENEURSHIP UNDER THE CONDITIONS OF DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION OF SOCIETY
summary: The article provides a comprehensive theoretical, methodological, and applied study of the formation and functioning of the system of state management mechanisms for the development of innovative entrepreneurship under the conditions of the total digital transformation of society. The essential and substantive characteristics of innovative entrepreneurship as a leading driver of national economic modernization are investigated. It is determined that digitalization acts as a catalyst for transformational processes, radically changing the architecture of business models, market structures, and tools of state regulatory policy. Based on a systematic approach, the system of state management mechanisms is structured into key blocks: regulatory, financial-economic, organizational-managerial, and information-technological. Special attention is paid to the analysis of the current state and trends in the development of innovative entrepreneurship in Ukraine. The dynamics of key indicators of innovative activity of domestic enterprises during 2018-2025 are analyzed, including the share of enterprises implementing innovations, the volume of funding for research and development (R&D), and the level of digital maturity of the business environment. Key destructive factors and barriers hindering innovative activity in the national space under martial law and post-war recovery are identified. The advanced experience of the European Union countries is studied in detail, in particular the models of Germany (the industrial platform 'Industry 4.0'), Estonia (the concept of the digital state 'e-Estonia' and digitalization of public services), and Finland (the ecosystem approach and financing tools of the Business Finland agency). The best European practices regarding the development of a network of digital innovation hubs, stimulation of venture investment, and implementation of tax incentives for knowledge-intensive enterprises are highlighted. A conceptual model for the modernization of public administration is proposed, which involves the integration of European standards, the expansion of public-private partnership instruments, the digitalization of administrative services for business, and the creation of a favorable regulatory landscape (regulatory 'sandboxes'). It is substantiated that the implementation of the proposed recommendations will ensure increasing the competitiveness of the national economy, accelerating European integration processes, and sustainable technological development of society.

title: THE IMPACT OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION ON ECONOMIC GROWTH: THE CASE OF THE LABOR MARKET AND PRODUCTIVITY
summary: The article analyzes the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital transformation on economic growth through the labor market and productivity channels. The study uses statistical-comparative, structural and logical analysis methods based on official and international statistical data for Uzbekistan for 2023–2026, the “Digital Uzbekistan – 2030” strategy and the Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence Technologies until 2030, as well as foreign empirical literature. The results show that AI affects growth in three ways: by raising total factor productivity, by reallocating tasks, and by creating new occupations. At the same time, the share of small business in employment (74.9%) is markedly higher than its share in gross domestic product (52.2%), which means that relative labor productivity in this sector is about 70% of the average level. This shows that diffusing AI tools precisely to low-productivity sectors is a major opportunity and, at the same time, a skills challenge. The article concludes with proposals on retraining of personnel, adoption of digital technologies in small business, data infrastructure, and measurement of the effects of AI.

title: CONTEMPORARY SOURCES OF INVESTMENT PROJECT FINANCING: BANK CREDIT, PRIVATE CAPITAL AND INTERNATIONAL FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS
summary: The study uses an integrative, theory-driven review of the corporate finance, financial intermediation and development finance literature. Sources are compared against six analytical criteria: cost of capital, tenor, risk allocation, information and monitoring requirements, accessibility, and non-financial value added.

title: Digital transformation, technological innovation, and e-sports: ISSF at a new stage of shooting sport development
summary: In the modern era, the survival of traditional sports disciplines is directly linked to their ability to adapt to a dynamic media environment. The International Shooting Sport Federation (ISSF) has entered a period of fundamental transformation, shifting from a closed technical discipline toward a high-demand global media product. The central challenge lies in changing the "cognitive perception" of shooting – transforming a process that appears static to an outside observer into an emotionally resonant and technologically accessible spectacle. This article analyzes the key directions of this process. First, it examines the diversification of content delivery through the aggressive scaling of digital presence and the exploration of new platforms. A vital aspect is the technological verification and increased transparency of officiating, achieved through the implementation of VAR objective control systems and "live aiming" shot visualization technologies. The study also investigates the integration of virtual reality and esports as a means of creating alternative "entry points" into the sport via digital simulators. Alongside these developments, the work analyses the associated risks and institutional consequences of this transformation. The implementation of innovations such as AI-driven hit analysis and VR tools fosters the necessary "immersive connection" between the athlete and the fan. This is critical for attracting sponsorship capital, as it allows dry technical data to be converted into engaging content. The findings are based on a comparative analysis of Redtorch reports (SportOnSocial 2025), official ISSF press releases, and current industry publications. title: FINANCIAL PERFORMANCE AND COMPANY SIZE ON COMPANY VALUE WITH CORPORATE SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY AS A MODERATING VARIABLE
summary: This study aims to analyze the effect of financial performance (Return on Equity/ROE) and company size on company value (Price to Book Value/PBV) with Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) as a moderating variable in metal mining subsector companies listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange for the 2021–2024 period. The study uses a quantitative approach with secondary data from 10 companies selected through purposive sampling (40 observations) and analyzed using panel data regression with EViews 12. The results show that financial performance and company size do not significantly influence company value, and CSR is not able to moderate the relationship. Therefore, further research is recommended to add other variables and expand the research object, while companies are expected to improve operational efficiency, performance, and transparency of financial reports to increase investor confidence.

title: Disentangling large-scale supply networks: f-HiCoNE framework for flow-hierarchical clustering via combinatorial Hodge decomposition
summary: Abstract Modern society relies on complex supply chains to sustain the flow of goods and services that are essential to daily life. While traditional supply chain theory assumes a clear, hierarchical flow from upstream suppliers to downstream customers, observable real-world transaction networks rarely exhibit this acyclic structure. Instead, detailed inter-firm data reveal that interwoven networks are heavily entangled by cyclic flows. Consequently, without appropriate partitioning of these massive inter-firm networks, the latent flow-hierarchical structures that are central to supply chain concepts remain obscure. To address this analytical challenge, we introduce the flow-Hierarchical Community Network Extraction (f-HiCoNE) framework. By applying combinatorial Hodge decomposition, this approach disentangles the complex inter-firm network by isolating the acyclic gradient flow to quantify the flow-hierarchical parts and partition the graph. By applying f-HiCoNE to a nationwide transaction dataset of approximately 650,000 firms, we extracted clusters exhibiting the flow-hierarchical organisation that supply-chain theory assumes. These clusters demonstrated strong flow-hierarchical organisation, wherein the upstream-downstream positioning of firms was well described by local scalar potentials, revealing distinct geographically localised industrial ecosystems. This study provides a map that could help firms understand their surrounding environment and locate their position within an inter-firm network and opens a new research avenue focused on flow-hierarchy clustering in supply chain analysis.

title: In search of transformative resilience in manufacturing supply chains: how and when digital platform capabilities and supply chain knowledge matter
summary: Purpose While recent Industry 5.0 paradigms emphasize human-centric and resilient manufacturing ecosystems supported by emerging technologies, the factors driving supply chain metaverse adoption (SCMA) and its mechanisms for enhancing transformative resilience remain underexplored. Unlike adaptive resilience, which focuses on recovery to pre-disruption states, transformative resilience involves fundamental reconfiguration enabling firms to emerge stronger from disruptions. Grounded in resource orchestration theory, this study examines how manufacturing firms combine digital platform capabilities (integration and reconstruction) and supply chain knowledge to drive SCMA and enhance transformative resilience. We investigate the mediating role of SCMA and the moderating effect of supply chain knowledge orchestration on the SCMA-resilience relationship. Design/methodology/approach We collected data from 300 senior managers across Ghanaian manufacturing firms using a two-wave survey design. Analysis of Moment Structures-based covariance structural equation modelingwas employed due to its suitability for theory-testing with well-established constructs, superior handling of measurement error, and ability to provide rigorous goodness-of-fit assessment. Hierarchical regression analysis examined the moderating effects. Common method bias was addressed through temporal separation, procedural remedies, and statistical tests (Harman’s single-factor test and the marker variable technique). Findings Both digital platform integration capability and reconstruction capability significantly drive SCMA. SCMA demonstrates substantial effects on transformative resilience, with effect sizes indicating strong practical significance beyond statistical significance. SCMA partially mediates the relationship between digital platform capabilities and transformative resilience. Critically, supply chain knowledge orchestration significantly strengthens the SCMA-resilience relationship, explaining an additional 12% of the variance, demonstrating that technology adoption alone is insufficient without knowledge-based capability development. Practical implications Manufacturing firms should adopt phased metaverse implementation strategies, first strengthening digital platform capabilities before full-scale deployment. Organizations must simultaneously develop knowledge orchestration mechanisms (establishing cross-functional learning structures, systematic knowledge capture processes, and virtual-to-physical translation capabilities) to maximize resilience benefits from metaverse investments. Originality/value This study advances supply chain resilience literature by demonstrating how metaverse technologies enable transformative (not merely adaptive) resilience through resource orchestration mechanisms. It extends Industry 5.0 scholarship by empirically validating the criticality of human-centric knowledge orchestration in amplifying advanced technology benefits. By revealing the conditional nature of metaverse value creation, the study provides novel theoretical insights into when and why digital platforms generate transformative outcomes, contributing to resource orchestration theory and digital transformation literature. The developing economy context offers rare empirical evidence of advanced technology adoption under resource constraints.

title: External Governance Shocks and Legitimacy Repair Through CSR
summary: ABSTRACT Research Question/Issue This study examines how firms adjust their corporate social responsibility (CSR) performance when product market competitors experience forced chief executive officer (CEO) turnover. Specifically, this study investigates whether peer CEO dismissals, as governance shocks signaling intensified board monitoring, trigger strategic CSR responses among rival firms. Research Findings/Insights Using US firm‐year observations from 2003 to 2020, this research documents that peer dismissals significantly increase firms' CSR performance, with effects concentrated in the social dimension rather than the environmental or governance dimensions. The positive relationship is stronger for firms with greater analyst coverage and for firms operating in more competitive markets, indicating that external scrutiny and competitive pressure strengthen strategic CSR adoption. Value‐creation tests demonstrate that CSR engagement in response to peer dismissals is associated with improved subsequent accounting performance, particularly in the social dimension. Theoretical/Academic Implications The findings support legitimacy theory over agency theory in explaining CSR motivations under governance pressure. This research demonstrates that CSR serves as an active legitimacy‐building mechanism rather than being constrained by governance discipline when firms face institutional pressures from peer governance failures. This research enriches the peer spillover literature by moving the focus from passive information transfer to active legitimacy management and extends executive turnover research by identifying CSR as a strategic response channel to external governance shocks. Practitioner/Policy Implications Boards and executives should recognize that peer governance failures create reputational risks requiring strategic stakeholder engagement. The evidence suggests that CSR practices can effectively mitigate legitimacy threats following industry‐wide governance shocks. Policymakers should recognize that governance failures in one firm create industry‐wide legitimacy threats that extend beyond the affected company and that the information environment plays a critical role in shaping how these threats spread across product markets.

title: Birds of a feather? Local gambling preferences and corporate debt maturity in China
summary: Although debt maturity is central to firms’ operations, how informal institutions such as local gambling preferences shape it remains unclear. Using a sample of A-share listed firms from 2008 to 2023, this paper explores whether and how local gambling preferences shape corporate debt maturity in China. Results show that stronger local gambling preferences are significantly associated with shorter corporate debt maturity, suggesting that firms in such regions tend to receive debt financing with shorter maturities. This result remains robust across a series of sensitivity and endogeneity tests, including instrumental variable approaches, omitted variables test, lagged term of gambling preferences, entropy matching, and other robustness checks. In addition, this effect can be attributed to a deteriorated information environment, worse corporate governance, and greater speculative investment. Consistent with these findings, this effect is more pronounced in firms with smaller assets, more financing constraints and those located in regions with lower financial development. Our study contributes to the broader literature on debt maturity by highlighting how informal institutions and local cultural norms can shape corporate financing behaviour.

title: Does Green Finance Drive Sustainable Banking? A PLS-SEM Analysis of CSR as a Mediator in Nepal's Commercial Banks
summary: Background: Green finance has emerged as an important mechanism for integrating environmental and social considerations into banking activities. As commercial banks increasingly adopt sustainable financing practices, understanding how green finance contributes to sustainable performance is particularly relevant in emerging economies such as Nepal. Purpose: This study examines the effect of green finance on the sustainable performance of commercial banks in Nepal, considering corporate social responsibility (CSR) as a mediating variable. Design/methodology/approach: The study adopts a descriptive and explanatory research design. Data were collected from 400 senior employees of commercial banks using non-probability purposive sampling. The study is grounded in the Triple Bottom Line Theory. Data were collected using KoboToolbox and analyzed using SmartPLS through partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Findings: The findings indicate that green finance has a significant positive relationship with all three dimensions of sustainability: environmental, economic, and social sustainability. Furthermore, CSR partially mediates the relationship between green finance and sustainable performance. The study also identifies challenges related to limited awareness and inadequate regulatory support for green finance practices. Conclusion: The study concludes that green finance significantly contributes to the sustainable performance of commercial banks in Nepal. Strengthening green financing practices, CSR initiatives, awareness, and regulatory support may help banks enhance their contribution to sustainable development.

title: Impact of Internal Audit on Corporate Governance in Deposit Money Banks in Nigeria
summary: The studies were focused on determining the relationship that exist between internal audit and corporate governance in deposit money banks in Nigeria. Specifically, the study’s objectives were to determine the relationship between internal audit function and the quality of corporate governance, the effect of internal audit reporting and independence on the quality of corporate governance, and the extent of the internal audit’s contribution to transparency and accountability. The survey research methodology was used in collecting data via a structured questionnaire, which was administered to employees in internal audit departments and other related departments such as compliance, risk management and finance in some selected deposit money banks in Nigeria. A total of 250 questionnaires were analysed using descriptive statistics and Pearson Product Moment Correlation and Multiple Regression Analyses. The findings revealed a strong positive and statistically significant relation between internal audit function and the quality of corporate governance (r =0.781, p<0.05). The influence of internal audit reporting and independence on the quality of corporate governance was found to be significant (R =0.677, F = 257.834, p<0.001). Both reporting and independence of internal audit influenced corporate governance quality although reporting played a dominant role as against independence of internal audit (regression coefficient of reporting: =0.491; regression coefficient of independence: =0.451). The ability of internal audit in enhancing transparency and accountability in deposit money banks in Nigeria was established (R = 0.724, F=663.552, p<0.001). The research concluded that, a more effective and independent internal audit in conjunction with thorough reporting greatly facilitates and enhance corporate governance among deposit money banks in Nigeria.

title: Digital Transformation and the Future of the Accounting Profession: Accountants' Emerging Digital Technology Roles
summary: The accounting profession is experiencing unprecedented transformation due to rapid advancements in digital technologies and the increasing complexity of modern business environments. Technologies such as artificial intelligence, big data analytics, cloud computing, blockchain, robotic process automation, enterprise resource planning systems, and cybersecurity solutions are redefining the traditional functions of accountants and creating new opportunities for professional value creation. This paper examines the evolving roles, responsibilities, and competencies of accountants in a technology-driven world and explores the implications of these developments for accounting education and professional practice in Nigeria. Adopting a narrative literature review and conceptual analysis approach, the study synthesizes evidence from scholarly literature, professional accounting reports, policy documents, and contemporary empirical studies. The review reveals that accountants are increasingly functioning as strategic business partners, data analysts, governance champions, risk management specialists, technology integrators, forensic accounting experts, tax advisors, sustainability reporting professionals, financial consultants, and cybersecurity collaborators. The study further finds that while technology has automated many routine accounting tasks, it has simultaneously increased the demand for higher-order competencies such as analytical thinking, digital literacy, professional judgment, strategic decision-making, communication, and ethical reasoning. The paper concludes that the future relevance of accountants depends largely on their ability to adapt to technological change through continuous learning and competency development. The study recommends curriculum reforms, enhanced professional training, stronger industry-academia collaboration, regulatory support, and sustained investments in digital capacity development to ensure that accountants remain relevant and effective in the evolving digital economy.

title: Institutional Capacity as a Mediating Mechanism between IFRS Implementation Inputs and Financial Reporting Quality: PLS-SEM Evidence from SMEs in Western Uganda
summary: Purpose: This article examines Institutional Capacity (IC) as the organisational transmission mechanism linking three IFRS implementation inputs - Accounting Systems Integration (ASI), Governance Practices (GOV), and Training and Resources (TR) to Financial Reporting Quality (RQ) among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Western Uganda. Design/methodology/approach: The study used a cross-sectional, quantitatively dominant embedded mixed-methods design. Primary survey data were collected from registered SMEs in Mbarara City during March 2026. Of 250 targeted SMEs, 203 complete cases were retained for the final SmartPLS 4 model. PLS-SEM was used to assess the measurement model, direct paths, specific indirect effects, explanatory power, and approximate model fit. Findings: ASI was the strongest observed predictor of IC (beta = 0.550), followed by GOV (beta = 0.378), whereas TR had a weak coefficient (beta = 0.038). RQ was positively associated with ASI (beta = 0.338), GOV (beta = 0.257), TR (beta = 0.199), and IC (beta = 0.224). The specific indirect effects through IC were 0.123 for ASI, 0.085 for GOV, and 0.008 for TR. The model explained 76.0% of the variance in IC and 77.7% of the variance in RQ (SRMR = 0.089; NFI = 0.966). The point estimate pattern is consistent with complementary partial mediation for ASI and GOV, while the mediated TR pathway is negligible. Because the final component-level bootstrap standard errors, p-values, and confidence intervals were not contained in the final dissertation output, formal mediation significance is intentionally not asserted. Originality/value: The study advances a capability-based interpretation of IFRS implementation by distinguishing implementation inputs from the institutional capacity through which they are converted into sustained reporting routines. In a resource- constrained SME setting, the results imply that systems and governance matter not only directly but also through their contribution to organisational capability.

title: Dynamics of Production‐ and Consumption‐Based Carbon Dioxide Emissions in China: The Influential Role of Energy Imports and Monetary Policy
summary: ABSTRACT As the world's largest CO 2 emitter and one of the largest energy importers, China encounters significant challenges in achieving its carbon neutrality target whilst ensuring environmental sustainability. Understanding how macroeconomic and energy‐related factors influence different dimensions of carbon emissions is therefore essential for designing effective climate policies. This study examines the effects of monetary policy and energy imports on aggregate carbon emissions, consumption‐based carbon emissions (COC) and production‐based carbon emissions (COP) in China over the period 1990–2020. The study employs the novel augmented autoregressive distributed lag (AARDL) approach to examine short run and long run relationship amongst variables. The empirical evidence demonstrates that monetary policy (i.e., real interest rate) has a positive relationship with aggregate CO 2 emissions and COC in the long run, whilst the relationship between monetary policy and COP is negative but statistically insignificant. Energy imports have a positive and significant impact on aggregate CO 2 emissions, COC and COP, in both the short and long run. Economic growth also contributes positively to all three emissions accounts, reflecting the environmental impact of China's energy‐intensive growth model. Therefore, the findings suggest that the integration of environmental goals into monetary policy, the promotion of green finance and the acceleration of the transition to renewable energy sources will be necessary to reduce CO 2 emissions and meet China's long‐term carbon neutrality.

title: Environmental, social and governance (ESG) performance, ethnicity and investment efficiency
summary: Purpose The paper aims to investigate the relationship between environmental, social and governance (ESG) performance and investment efficiency in Malaysia. Subsequently, the paper investigates whether ethnicity, proxied by Bumiputera directors, moderates the relationship. Design/methodology/approach This study uses publicly listed firms on Bursa Malaysia from 2017 to 2022, yielding a sample of 216 firm-year observations. The authors used multivariate ordinary least squares regression to test the relationship and to correct for the selection bias, the Heckman two-stage selection bias and lag ESG test were used. Findings The study finds that higher ESG performance reduces investment efficiency. The finding supports the trade-off hypothesis and suggests the possibility of managerial opportunism, with managers investing in ESG activities for self-interest. The study further finds that Bumiputera directors, a proxy for ethnicity, weaken the negative relationship between ESG performance and investment efficiency. The weaker negative relationship indicates that the presence of Bumiputera directors mitigates information asymmetry by improving disclosure. The results remain robust to a series of additional and endogeneity tests. The findings have important implications for practitioners and policymakers: ESG effectiveness depends not only on the extent of disclosure but also on the governance structure. Originality/value By highlighting the role of Bumiputera directors, this study reveals that governance structures rooted in local institutional dynamics can significantly shape the relationship between ESG performance and investment efficiency.

title: Assessing Supply Chain Demand-Supply Imbalances and Their Impact on MSME Performance Using AI-Driven Analytics
summary: Micro, Small and Medium sized Enterprises (MSMEs) have a significant contribution in the area of economic development, employment generation and industrial growth.But, the frequent demand-supplier imbalance in supply chains has a significant impact on the efficiency, the profit and sustainability of the supply chain.The present study examines the effect of the imbalance in demand and supply in the supply chain on the performance of MSMEs listed and unlisted.The research combines Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), and Graph-Theoretic Supply Chain Analysis to model demand forecasting and supply chain disruptions.The mismatches between market demand and production supply are proposed to be quantified by proposing a Demand-Supply Imbalance Index (DSII).The analyzed data are obtained from 210 MSMEs and used structural equation modeling (SEM), random forest regression and graph centrality algorithms.The results show that the accuracy of demand forecasts, connectivity of the supplier network and inventory optimization have a significant impact on MSME performance.The accuracy of AI-based predictive models exceeds that of traditional forecasting methods, with a prediction accuracy of more than 91%.The proposed Graph Supply Chain Resilience Model pinpoints key nodes that cause disruptions in the supply chain.The study offers actionable strategies for MSMEs to use AI-powered decision-making to enhance their supply chain resilience and business outcomes.

title: AI readiness and digital pedagogical competence as enablers of innovations in environmental management within higher education institutions: evidence from Vietnam
summary: Purpose This study aims to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) readiness and digital pedagogical competence (DPC) are associated with lecturers’ perceptions of digital environmental governance innovation (DEGI) and perceived environmental performance in higher education institutions (HEIs). Moving beyond isolated green technologies, the study adopts a governance-oriented perspective to explain how individual digital capabilities among academic staff are linked to perceived sustainability-related outcomes through digitally enabled environmental governance innovation. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a quantitative research design using survey data collected from 1,525 academic staff working in Vietnamese HEIs. Partial least squares structural equation modelling was used to test the proposed capability–governance–perception framework and to examine both direct and indirect relationships among the constructs. Findings The findings indicate that AI readiness (artificial intelligence readiness) is positively associated with DPC and lecturers’ perceptions of DEGI. DPC is also positively associated with governance innovation. Most importantly, lecturers’ perceptions of DEGI are strongly associated with perceived environmental performance and indicate a statistically significant indirect association between AIR and perceived environmental outcomes within the specified model. Research limitations/implications This study is based on cross-sectional, self-reported survey data from a single national context, which limits causal inference and statistical generalisability. The findings should therefore be interpreted as perception-based associations rather than evidence of objectively measured institutional environmental improvement. Future research could adopt longitudinal, comparative, multi-source or objective-indicator designs. Practical implications The findings suggest that HEIs should move beyond technology adoption alone and invest in human digital capabilities, sustainability dashboards, environmental data reporting systems and governance structures. Strengthening AIR and DPC among academic staff may support digitally mediated governance innovations for environmental management. Social implications By highlighting governance innovation as a perception-based pathway linking digital capabilities to perceived environmental performance, this study offers insights for HEIs seeking to strengthen their sustainability responsibilities. Digitally enabled environmental governance may support broader sustainability transitions, provided it is embedded within accountable institutional practices. Originality/value This study offers empirical evidence linking individual digital capabilities to perceived environmental management outcomes in higher education through governance innovation. It extends sustainability and digital transformation research by positioning AIR and DPC as enablers of perceived digitally driven environmental governance, particularly within a Global South context.

title: Industry 4.0 readiness in electrical companies
summary: This study examines the readiness of electrical companies to adopt Industry 4.0 principles, focusing on the degree of product customization and communication practices within customer and supply chains. Using a questionnaire survey via GoogleForms, data was collected from 28 companies in the electrical industry. The results showed that 63% of companies offer full product customization, indicating advanced technology integration, while 23% of companies only allow partial customization, indicating a transitional phase towards Industry 4.0 adoption. However, 14% stick to fixed product portfolios, reflecting limited flexibility and readiness for digital transformation. The communication analysis further revealed that most companies still rely on traditional methods such as electronic and telephone communication to interact with suppliers and customers, with only 10% achieving fully automated digital integration. This study highlights significant gaps in digitalisation and provides useful insights in terms of technology adoption and communication strategies in line with Industry 4.0 principles.

title: Evaluation of Indonesia’s Legal and Institutional Framework for Environmental Pollution Mitigation
summary: Environmental pollution is a major challenge to Indonesia’s environmental governance, despite its relatively comprehensive legal framework, due to pressures from urbanization, industrialization, mining, waste, air pollution, and deforestation. This study examines the effectiveness of Indonesia’s legal and institutional framework in addressing environmental pollution through comparison with the legal systems of Uganda and East Africa. The study employs a normative legal method with statutory and comparative approaches to Uganda, particularly the National Environment Management Authority (NEMA). This study demonstrates, first, Law No. 6 of 2023 potentially weakens environmental protection through the centralization of EIA, restrictions on public access, reduced recognition of local wisdom, and uncertainty regarding strict liability. Second, institutional changes under Law No. 6 of 2023 create ambiguity in the division of authority and coordination of environmental oversight between central and regional governments, potentially creating gaps in oversight and accountability. Third, based on comparison with Uganda, this study recommends strengthening risk-based EIA, access to information and public participation, pollution control, strict liability, and integrated environmental oversight and enforcement oriented towards environmental restoration. Thus, the study aims to strengthen Indonesia’s environmental governance towards ecologically just pollution control

title: Corporate Data Tracking in the European Union: Regulatory Gaps, Commercial Incentives, and Public-Sector Access
summary: The European Union combines unusually extensive formal protections for personal data with a digital economy in which commercial tracking, profiling, data brokerage and automated inference remain widespread. This paper examines why the existence of strong privacy law does not necessarily produce the disappearance of large-scale commercial data collection. The analysis focuses on three interacting mechanisms: limits on supervisory capacity, the practical difficulty of meaningful choice within complex digital data ecosystems, and the secondary operational value that commercially generated datasets may possess for public authorities. Drawing upon evidence from the European Union Agency for Fundamental Rights (FRA), the European Commission, the European Data Protection Board (EDPB), Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) jurisprudence, and contemporary reporting on commercially sourced intelligence, the paper argues that persistent corporate tracking can coexist with strong legal protections without requiring assumptions of deliberate regulatory collusion. The paper develops an institutional explanation in which economic incentives, fragmented responsibility, finite supervisory resources, complex commercial data supply chains, and secondary public-sector utility collectively contribute to the persistence of large-scale data collection. The resulting gap between formal privacy protection and practical control is examined as an institutional phenomenon rather than a conspiratorial one. The study concludes that strong privacy law and extensive commercial data tracking are not necessarily contradictory. Instead, they reflect the interaction of legal frameworks, market structures, technological complexity, institutional capacity, and the continuing value of personal data within both commercial and public-sector contexts. This paper will form part of our policy proposal for 2029/31 elections

title: Water–Energy–Food Nexus Approaches to Climate Change Adaptation in Sub-Saharan Africa: Mapping Evidence from Integrated Resource Management Practices
summary: Climate change poses significant threats to water availability, energy security, and food production in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), undermining sustainable development and increasing the vulnerability of communities that are dependent on climate-sensitive resources. In response, the Water–Energy–Food (WEF) nexus has emerged as an integrated framework for addressing the interdependencies among these critical sectors while enhancing climate resilience. This study mapped and synthesized existing evidence on WEF nexus approaches to climate change adaptation in SSA through a scoping review. Guided by the Arksey and O’Malley framework and reported in accordance with the PRISMA-ScR guidelines, the review involved a systematic search of Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, Wiley Online Library, Google Scholar, and relevant grey literature sources. The findings revealed a growing body of research on WEF nexus-based adaptation, with studies predominantly concentrated in Southern Africa, particularly South Africa. Major integrated resource management approaches identified include climate-smart agriculture, integrated water-resources management, renewable energy integration, nexus-based planning, governance and policy integration, and community-based adaptation. Reported outcomes include enhanced climate resilience; improved water, energy, and food security; strengthened livelihoods; increased resource-use efficiency; and improved institutional coordination. However, implementation remains constrained by fragmented governance systems, limited financing, inadequate data, technical capacity deficits, and weak stakeholder engagement. Key enabling factors include policy coherence, institutional collaboration, technological innovation, climate finance, and capacity-building. The review concludes that the WEF nexus provides a valuable framework for advancing climate adaptation and sustainable resource management in SSA.

title: Sweet Heaven Bakery Shopping System
summary: This project outlines the development of a modern, artisanal bakery shop designedto bridge traditional baking techniques with contemporary consumer preferences. The venturefocuses on producing high-quality, preservative-free baked goods ranging from sourdoughbreads to specialty pastries using locally sourced, organic ingredients to appeal to health-conscious and premium markets. To ensure operational efficiency and market viability, theproject integrates a robust business strategy combining an inviting brick-and-mortar storefrontwith a streamlined digital ordering platform for local delivery and catering. By analyzingmarket demand, establishing reliable supply chains, and implementing sustainable waste-reduction practices, the project aims to cultivate a loyal local customer base while maintainingstrong financial profitability and scalability in a competitive food and beverage sector.

title: Geopolitical risk and accounting conservatism: does financial reporting opacity matter? Evidence from an emerging market
summary: As global markets increasingly navigate extreme external shocks, understanding how macroeconomic turbulence reshapes corporate financial reporting strategies remains a critical challenge for stakeholders. This study investigates the empirical relationship between macro-level geopolitical risk (GPR) and accounting conservatism (AC), while examining the moderating role of financial reporting opacity (FRO) in an emerging market setting. Using a panel data sample of 100 non-financial Egyptian Exchange companies spanning 2018–2024 (700 firm-year observations), the analysis employs a random-effects panel regression with year- and firm-clustered standard errors to accommodate the macro-level nature of the GPR index. The findings provide robust empirical evidence that GPR is positively associated with AC. Furthermore, FRO acts as a key moderating factor, significantly strengthening this positive association. This demonstrates that under heightened macro-geopolitical exposure, accounting conservatism strongly aligns with strategic shock absorption and compensatory signaling. The demand for conservative reporting increases more steeply in response to GPR when firm-level financial information is ambiguous, bridging critical information gaps. These empirical associations remain consistent across sensitivity and endogeneity specifications. Overall, the findings offer vital implications for regulators enhancing transparency mandates during crises, and for investors utilizing conservatism as an indicator of managerial prudence in volatile economies.

title: Assessing enablers for smart technologies in maritime and shipping logistics: a GINA approach
summary: Purpose This study aims to assess the key enablers facilitating the adoption of smart technologies in maritime and shipping logistics using the Grey Influence Analysis (GINA) approach. As maritime supply chains become digitalised at a fast pace, technologies such as Artificial Intelligence, Internet of Things, Blockchain, Big Data analytics and Digital Twins have become significant drivers of efficiency, sustainability and resilience in operations; however, their successful implementation is contingent on an interconnected set of technological, environmental, economic, ecological and social enablers. Design/methodology/approach The paper identifies the major enablers influencing the adoption of smart technology in maritime logistics through an extensive literature review and professional validation. Expert opinion was collected using a structured questionnaire, and the GINA methodology was applied to identify causal relationships and determine the relative importance of each enabler. This methodology enables the analysis of a large number of responses without information loss, addressing the shortcomings of conventional approaches such as Interpretive Structural Modelling and DEMATEL. Findings The findings identify the most potent enablers that play a significant role in the digital transformation of maritime logistics systems. Practical implications The insights generated will inform policymakers, port actors and logistics managers of the strategic areas of interest for investment and for devising sustainable, smart logistics ecosystems. Originality/value By integrating intelligent technologies with a rigorous causal analysis approach, the paper contributes to the current body of knowledge on maritime digitalization.

title: Forecasting Climate and Extreme Weather Disruption Risk at Critical Logistics Nodes: Ports, Corridors, and Inland Gateways
summary: Critical logistics nodes, including major seaports, inland waterway locks, rail gateways, and key highway corridors, concentrate the physical movement of goods that sustain the United States economy and support national security supply chains. Extreme weather events, including hurricanes, flooding, extreme heat, drought related low water, and winter storms, have repeatedly disrupted operations at these nodes, producing cascading delays, inventory shortages, and elevated costs. As the frequency and intensity of certain extremes change, the value of anticipatory disruption forecasting rises. This research project examines how meteorological forecasts, historical disruption records, node specific vulnerability attributes, and network dependency data can be combined into practical early warning and impact estimation tools for logistics planners. The project outlines indicator construction, impact scoring, scenario based stress testing of network consequences, and decision linkages to pre positioning, modal shift, and inventory buffering. The contribution is an applied structure that transportation agencies, port authorities, defense logistics organizations, and private network operators can adapt to improve readiness for weather driven supply stress without requiring perfect event prediction.

title: Faktor-Faktor yang Mempengaruhi Pemilihan Kantor Akuntan pada Perusahaan Perbankan
summary: This study aims to examine the effect of foreign ownership, independent commissioners, and audit committee effectiveness on the selection of Public Accounting Firms (PAFs) in banking companies listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) during 2020–2024. This study uses a quantitative method with secondary data obtained from companies’ annual reports. The sample was selected using purposive sampling based on predetermined criteria. The data were then analyzed using logistic regression. The results show that foreign ownership has no effect on PAF selection. Independent commissioners also have no effect on PAF selection. Meanwhile, audit committee effectiveness has a positive and significant effect on PAF selection. These results indicate that companies with more effective audit committees tend to have a greater likelihood of selecting Big Four PAFs. Therefore, audit committee effectiveness is one of the factors related to a company’s decision in selecting the PAF to be appointed

title: Is corporate social responsibility disclosure associated with stock liquidity? Evidence from Vietnam
summary: Purpose This study aims to examine whether corporate social responsibility disclosure (CSRD) is associated with stock liquidity in Vietnam’s prescribed reporting setting. Design/methodology/approach Using 2,476 firm-year observations for 499 non-financial firms during 2015–2019, the study estimates firm and year fixed-effects models with firm-clustered standard errors. CSRD is measured by score and percentage; liquidity is measured by effective and quoted spreads. First-difference and one-year-lagged specifications assess robustness. Findings Neither CSRD measure is significantly associated with either spread after firm-specific heterogeneity and common annual conditions are controlled for. The findings indicate that greater disclosure intensity alone does not necessarily reduce spread-based trading costs when reporting does not ensure comparable, credible and decision-useful information. Research limitations/implications The study is confined to Vietnamese non-financial firms within a specific timeframe. Future research could examine multiple countries, alternative liquidity measures and the credibility and investor use of disclosed information. Practical implications Firms should not assume that increasing disclosure quantity will reduce spread-based trading costs. The findings emphasize reporting comparability, consistency, assurance and enforcement. Originality/value Evidence on CSRD and stock-market liquidity remains mixed. Unlike positive findings based on externally assessed transparency, report events, global reporting initiative (GRI) adoption or mandatory reforms, this study finds no robust association for observed GRI-based disclosure intensity in Vietnam, consistent with evidence from Jordan. Disclosure volume may therefore convey a weaker market signal than standardized or salient disclosure changes.

title: THE IMPLEMENTATION OF ESG PRINCIPLES IN SUKUK INNOVATION: CHALLENGES AND OPPORTUNITIES
summary: The growing global emphasis on Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) principles has significantly influenced the development of sustainable finance, including within the Islamic financial system. Sukuk, as a key instrument of Islamic capital markets, holds substantial potential to support sustainable and inclusive economic growth when aligned with ESG principles. This paper examines the implementation of ESG principles in sukuk innovation, with a particular focus on the challenges and opportunities faced by Islamic financial institutions and regulators. Using a qualitative and conceptual approach, this study analyzes the compatibility between ESG frameworks and the foundational principles of Islamic finance, as well as recent developments in innovative sukuk structures such as green sukuk, social sukuk, and sustainability-linked sukuk. The findings indicate that while ESG principles are largely consistent with the objectives of Shariah (maqasid al-shariah), several challenges remain. These include the lack of standardized ESG measurement and reporting, regulatory fragmentation, Shariah governance complexities, and limited market awareness. Despite these challenges, the integration of ESG principles into sukuk innovation presents significant opportunities. ESG-based sukuk can enhance market competitiveness, attract socially responsible investors, strengthen transparency, and reinforce the role of Islamic finance in achieving sustainable development goals. This paper contributes to the ongoing discourse on sustainable Islamic finance by providing insights into how ESG-oriented sukuk innovation can be effectively developed to support long-term economic sustainability and inclusive growth.

title: Regulatory structure and incentives for financial crime in digital asset markets: An analysis of expected utility from a legal and economic perspective
summary: The expansion of fintech and digital asset markets has given rise to new forms of financial crime, particularly money laundering through sophisticated and difficult-to-detect digital asset transactions. Despite many countries having developed clear legal frameworks and penalties, money laundering persists. This situation is not due to inadequate legal provisions, but rather reflects the limitations of regulatory measures that have failed to modify the incentive structures of offenders at the decision-making stage. This research presents a novel contribution by performing the first structural analysis of expected utility in the context of digital assets. It integrates Expected Utility and Deterrence Theory with a legal analysis framework, using comparative case studies from Mt. Gox, Terra–LUNA, Terraform Labs, and ZipMEX. The study found that combining services, cross-chain bridges, and DeFi protocols significantly reduces the probability of detection ( p ) and the cost of the offender ( C ) , independent of state-imposed penalties. Therefore, adding legal provisions or penalties cannot alter the calculation of the offender’s expected utility. To be effective, Anti-Money Laundering/Combating the Financing of Terrorism (AML/CFT) measures must structurally reduce offenders’ incentives by increasing the probability of detection and raising the cost of criminal activity, coupled with robust international cooperation mechanisms.

title: AI Adoption and Remote Teaching Supply Chain Efficiency
summary: With the ongoing digital transformation of education and the pervasive integration of artificial intelligence, the remote teaching supply chain has emerged as a critical backbone supporting the flow of online educational resources, the delivery of instructional services, and the implementation of talent cultivation. Optimizing the efficiency of this supply chain is essential for addressing key practical challenges, including resource misallocation, procedural redundancies, and insufficient coordination in online education. Grounded in technology acceptance theory, this study investigates how basic artificial intelligence adoption and advanced artificial intelligence adoption influence remote teaching supply chain efficiency, as well as the moderating effect of the digital technology environment. Based on an analysis of 206 valid survey responses from practitioners in universities, vocational colleges, and online education institutions, both basic and advanced artificial intelligence adoption exert positive effects on remote teaching supply chain efficiency. In addition, the digital technology environment positively moderates the relationships between basic artificial intelligence adoption and supply chain efficiency, as well as between advanced artificial intelligence adoption and supply chain efficiency. Finally, theoretical guidance and managerial implications are provided for the intelligent development of educational institutions and platforms, as well as for the optimization of remote teaching supply chains.

title: Built, but not replaced: The policy failure behind the UK's ageing greenhouse sector
summary: Societal Impact Statement Glass greenhouse horticulture is a highly productive but often overlooked component of UK agricultural, environmental and food policy, with significant potential to contribute to food security, public health and climate resilience. This paper argues that the ageing greenhouse estate reflects long‐term policy misalignment and the absence of conditions required for sustained investment and renewal. By reframing greenhouse production as infrastructure, it highlights opportunities to better align food production with energy systems, public procurement and spatial planning. Such integration could reduce import dependence, stabilise supply chains and strengthen links between domestic food production (incl. nursery plants) and public‐sector procurement, particularly within institutions such as the NHS and local authorities, supporting a more resilient and sustainable model of domestic production. Summary The United Kingdom's glass greenhouse horticulture sector is characterised by ageing infrastructure, with more than 70% of commercial greenhouse structures now over 40 years old and many constructed under technological and economic conditions that differ substantially from those of modern greenhouse production. This opinion piece argues that this is not simply the result of market conditions or technological change but the outcome of a long‐term policy trajectory in which food horticulture has been consistently included within agricultural frameworks without being recognised as a distinct, capital‐ and energy‐intensive system. A historical perspective is used to show how post‐war policy alignment enabled large‐scale infrastructure development, followed by a sustained period of underinvestment linked to policy frameworks that were poorly aligned with the capital, energy and infrastructure requirements of greenhouse production. Although recent policy developments signal renewed interest in controlled environment production, they remain insufficiently integrated. Reframing greenhouse horticulture as infrastructure provides a basis for aligning policy across energy, planning and procurement, and for addressing the risks associated with continued reliance on ageing systems and imported supply.

title: Algorithmic Monopoly: New Challenges for Indonesian Business Competition Law Enforcement in the Face of Digital Platform Dominance
summary: Background: The digital economy has transformed business competition by positioning algorithms, data, artificial intelligence, and network effects as key sources of market power. This development has enabled algorithmic monopolies, in which digital platforms exert substantial control over market access and interactions, posing challenges to Indonesia’s conventional competition law framework.Objective: This study examines the characteristics of algorithmic monopolies, identifies limitations in dominant-position regulation under Law Number 5 of 1999, compares regulatory approaches in the European Union, the United States, and the OECD, and proposes a reconstructed concept of algorithm-based market dominance for Indonesian competition law.Methods: This normative legal research applies statutory, conceptual, comparative, and case approaches. Legal materials comprising regulations, scholarly literature, policy documents, and digital competition law developments were qualitatively examined using a prescriptive-analytical method.Results: The findings reveal that the existing dominant-position framework inadequately addresses market power derived from algorithms, data control, and network effects, creating a normative gap. Comparative analysis demonstrates more adaptive approaches through the European Union’s Digital Markets Act, modernized U.S. antitrust policies, and OECD algorithmic governance initiatives. Accordingly, this study proposes algorithmic market dominance as an assessment framework encompassing control over data and algorithms, network effects, user dependence, self-preferencing, and digital barriers to entry.Conclusion: This reconstruction provides a conceptual basis for regulatory reform and KPPU enforcement guidelines responsive to digital-market dynamics while strengthening competition, innovation, fairness, legal certainty, and accountability in Indonesia’s digital economy.

title: Scaling paludiculture: stakeholder perspectives on adoption and enabling conditions in England
summary: Paludiculture, the cultivation of wetland species on rewetted peatlands, is increasingly promoted as a nature-based solution for climate mitigation, biodiversity restoration and peat conservation; however, its adoption remains limited in the United Kingdom. This study examines stakeholder perspectives on the adoption of paludiculture and the enabling conditions required to support its scale-up. Drawing on 36 photo-elicitation interviews with farmers, land managers, conservation organisations, researchers, and policymakers, the study explores how stakeholders interpret the ecological, economic, and socio-cultural implications of transitioning from drained peatland agriculture to wetland-based systems. Results indicate widespread recognition of environmental benefits, including greenhouse gas mitigation, flood regulation, and habitat restoration. However, adoption is constrained by concerns related to food security, land valuation, regulatory complexity, and underdeveloped markets. Stakeholders also highlight gaps in policy frameworks, with existing financial mechanisms perceived as short-term and poorly adapted to peatland systems. Market development, long-term policy support, and a strengthened evidence base emerge as critical enabling conditions, requiring coordinated policy, sustained investment, and cross-sector collaboration to support viable supply chains and demand. Aligning policy design with locally grounded knowledge and stakeholder needs is essential to enable effective environmental management.

title: INNOVATIVE MANAGEMENT TOOLS AND DIGITAL TECHNOLOGIES IN CHARITABLE ORGANIZATIONS
summary: The article examines current trends in the use of innovative management instruments and digital technologies by charitable organizations under wartime and post-war transformations in Ukraine. It substantiates digital transformation as a strategic basis for improving organizational efficiency, transparency, accountability, resilience and the capacity to generate sustainable social impact. The study applies a systems approach, comparative and structural-functional analysis, synthesis, generalization and graphical modelling, and draws on scientific publications, analytical reports and the practices of leading Ukrainian charitable organizations. The evolution of digitalization from the automation of individual processes to an integrated model of strategic management is identified. The main instruments are systematized, including digital fundraising, CRM systems, data-driven management, artificial intelligence, cloud technologies, project management systems, digital accountability and social impact assessment. A conceptual model of digital transformation and a digitalization risk matrix are developed, while digital development models used by leading Ukrainian charitable organizations are compared. The findings demonstrate that the integrated application of digital technologies improves decision-making, donor and stakeholder engagement, fundraising effectiveness, transparency, operational flexibility and organizational sustainability. Particular attention is paid to digital risks related to cybersecurity, data protection, technological dependence, insufficient digital competencies and disruption of digital infrastructure. The scientific novelty lies in developing a comprehensive approach to digital transformation that integrates external transformation drivers, digital technologies, innovative management instruments, organizational processes, risk management and social impact outcomes within a unified strategic management framework. The practical significance of the results consists in their applicability to the development of digital transformation strategies, improvement of fundraising and accountability mechanisms, management of digital risks, strengthening of organizational resilience and enhancement of the social effectiveness of charitable organizations during wartime and post-war recovery.

title: Productivity Narratives and Environmental Blind Spots: A Systematic Review of How Organizations Weigh Environmental Criteria When Adopting Generative AI
summary: Generative AI (GenAI) spreads through organizations faster than any shared method for weighing its environmental cost. Two literatures study the phenomenon from opposite ends. Adoption research explains why firms take up GenAI; environmental research measures the energy, water, and carbon it consumes. Whether the first treats the findings of the second as decision criteria remains unexamined. This systematic review asks how organizations incorporate environmental criteria into GenAI adoption and tests the proposition that productivity and modernization narratives dominate adoption and limit environmental governance. A TITLE-ABS-KEY search combining GenAI, adoption, and environmental terms yielded a corpus of 59 sources; main findings were extracted for 46 and grouped by the role each study assigns to the environment. Fourteen studies explain adoption through readiness, institutional pressure, top management support, and ethical leadership. None records ecological cost as a determinant, while six model ethics explicitly. Eleven studies treat environmental performance as an outcome of adoption. Twenty-one measures the environmental burden or proposes instruments to govern it, yet only six tie those instruments to organizational decisions. The evidence supports the proposition with one qualification: environmental criteria are absent from adoption models, which is different from absent from practice. The review separates two meanings of "environmental" that the literature conflates, consolidates candidate decision criteria, and sets an agenda for testing ecological cost as an antecedent of adoption.

title: How International Trade and Global Value Chains Reshape Environmental Sustainability
summary: The expansion of international trade and global value chains has transformed the geographical organization of production while redistributing environmental pressures across countries, sectors and stages of production. This paper examines the relationship between trade integration, global value-chain participation and environmental sustainability through three complementary dimensions. First, it considers how trade liberalization affects pollution, embodied carbon, natural-resource use, water pressures and biodiversity through scale, composition and technique effects. Second, it examines the environmental consequences of global value-chain participation, focusing on value-chain position, technological upgrading, supplier capabilities, lead-firm governance and multi-tier sustainability management. Third, it considers the institutional mechanisms through which trade policy can contribute to environmental governance, including environmental provisions in trade agreements, carbon border adjustment mechanisms and trade in environmental goods. The literature indicates that international integration does not produce a uniform environmental outcome. Trade can expand production and shift ecological pressures across borders, but it can also promote cleaner technologies, productivity improvements and environmental upgrading when appropriate regulatory, technological and organizational conditions are present. Sustainable globalization therefore depends on the interaction between trade policies, domestic environmental regulation, value-chain governance, technological capacity and international cooperation. Environmental policy must consequently address both territorial emissions and the ecological pressures embodied in internationally fragmented production and consumption networks.

title: Design and Development of an Automated Bursary Management System for Federal Polytechnics in North-East Nigeria: A Case Study of Federal Polytechnic Bauchi
summary: Financial administration in tertiary institutions involves high-volume transactions, multiple approval stages, financial records, reconciliation activities, payroll, budgeting and reporting. Where these processes depend on fragmented or paper-based procedures, delays, duplicate records, weak traceability and reporting inconsistencies can arise. This study presents the design and development of an Automated Bursary Management System (ABMS) developed for Federal Polytechnic Bauchi as a case study relevant to Federal Polytechnics in North East Nigeria. The study adopts a design-oriented information-systems approach and an acceptance-focused user evaluation. The system integrates student-fee management, revenue collection, payroll, budgeting, procurement payments, expenditure control, bank reconciliation, financial reporting, user management, role-based access control and audit trails within a web-based environment. For the institutional user-acceptance analysis, the 120-response UAT dataset confirmed for the Federal Polytechnic Bauchi ABMS evaluation was subjected to data-quality screening. Twelve item-level missing responses were identified, and three straight-line response patterns were excluded. Construct scores were computed from available valid items, leaving 117 respondents for inferential analysis. Reliability was satisfactory, with Cronbach’s alpha values ranging from .835 to .897. Mean scores were 2.99 for perceived usefulness, 2.93 for perceived ease of use, 3.00 for security readiness and 2.92 for system use/acceptance. Multiple regression showed that perceived ease of use (β = .514, p < .001) and security readiness (β = .431, p < .001) were significant positive predictors of system use/acceptance, whereas perceived usefulness was marginal and did not reach the conventional .05 level (β = .124, p = .052). The model explained 59.8% of the variance in system use/acceptance. The statistical findings reported in this article are based on the institutional UAT records used for the Federal Polytechnic Bauchi ABMS evaluation and are presented as evidence from the participating users. The study contributes a context-specific architecture and an empirically structured evaluation of the developed system for digital bursary transformation in Nigerian polytechnics.

title: AUDIT COMMITTEE GOVERNANCE AND FINANCIAL REPORTING TIMELINESS OF LISTED NON-FINANCIAL FIRMS IN NIGERIA
summary: This study examined the effect of audit committee governance on the timeliness of financial reporting in selected listed non-financial firms in Nigeria, with attention to auditor tenure as an explanatory variable. Using a sample of 80 firms from a population of 102 over 2015-2024 (800 firm-year observations), the study measured audit report lag as the dependent variable and assessed audit committee independence, financial expertise, gender diversity, size, and meeting frequency as explanatory variables. Secondary data from annual reports were analysed using descriptive statistics, Shapiro-Wilk normality tests, Spearman correlation, Levin-Lin-Chu panel unit root tests, and Panel Corrected Standard Errors regression, with all five committee attributes and auditor tenure entered jointly in a single model. Findings revealed that gender diversity and meeting frequency significantly reduced audit report lag, while independence, financial expertise, committee size, and auditor tenure showed no significant direct effect once all attributes were considered jointly, and the model's explanatory power was modest (R-squared = 1.77%). The study confirmed the applicability of agency and resource dependence theories, showing that gender diverse, actively engaged committees are the strongest observed drivers of reporting efficiency in this sample. It is recommended that firms prioritise gender diversity and a disciplined meeting calendar as practical levers for reporting timeliness, while continuing to strengthen independence and expertise on the wider governance rationale, even though this sample did not detect a significant effect for either. These insights offer practical guidance for regulators, managers, and investors in enhancing audit quality and market confidence.

title: THE ROLE OF CORPORATE SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY IN MODERATING THE EFFECT OF FINANCIAL PERFORMANCE AND CAPITAL STRUCTURE ON FIRM VALUE
summary: Basic Materials companies in Indonesia face challenges in maintaining firm value stability in the post-pandemic period due to fluctuations in financial performance and changes in capital structure. Firm value, measured by Price to Book Value (PBV), is influenced by Return on Assets (ROA) and Debt to Equity Ratio (DER). In addition, Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) disclosure is considered capable of influencing investor perceptions and stakeholder trust. This study aims to analyze the effect of financial performance and capital structure on firm value with CSR as a moderating variable. The data used are secondary data obtained from annual reports and financial statements of 13 Basic Materials companies listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange during the 2021–2024 period. The analysis was conducted using panel data regression and Moderated Regression Analysis (MRA) through EViews 10 software. The results show that financial performance and capital structure do not significantly affect firm value. Furthermore, CSR is unable to moderate the relationship between financial performance and firm value, as well as the relationship between capital structure and firm value. Companies are advised to improve profitability management, optimize capital structure, and strengthen CSR disclosure quality to enhance firm value and stakeholder confidence.

title: Strengthening Tarif Principles Embeddedness in Pertamina's STK: A Governance Assessment of Framework
summary: Background: Corporate governance is effective only when policy-level principles are translated into observable operational requirements. In large state-owned enterprises, strong formal governance can coexist with incomplete procedural embeddedness, creating a governance translation gap. Objective: This study evaluates the embeddedness of Transparency, Accountability, Responsibility, Independency, and Fairness (TARIF) principles in PT Pertamina (Persero)’s Sistem Tata Kerja (STK), using procurement planning as a pilot case. Methods: An action-research-oriented qualitative case design combined systematic document analysis, corporate risk and governance records, and practitioner validation. Nine procedural elements were mapped against five TARIF principles, producing 45 element–principle combinations rated as present, partial, enhancement opportunity, or not applicable. Results: Overall governance coverage was 56%. Responsibility was the strongest principle, at 89%, whereas Independency was the weakest, at 11%, revealing gaps in conflict-of-interest controls, separation of duties, and independent review. The most consequential gaps occurred in needs identification and supporting documentation for vendor selection. Alternative C+ received the strongest overall evaluation. Conclusion: The findings show that governance quality should be assessed not only through policy-level compliance but also through explicit procedural mechanisms. The TARIF-to-STK Governance Enhancement Framework operationalizes the policy-to-procedure distance and provides a structured basis for targeted improvement. Theoretically, it extends governance assessment toward procedure-level embeddedness; practically, it supports repeatable STK review and prioritization. Because the evidence derives from a single procurement-planning case, broader applicability requires validation across other STKs and longitudinal assessment of implementation effects.

title: Effect of Regulatory Requirements on Financial Fraud Detection Among Listed Deposit Money Banks in Nigeria
summary: This study examined the effect of regulatory requirements on financial fraud detection among listed deposit money banks in Nigeria. The research specifically investigated the impact of five key regulatory requirements: anti-money laundering (AML) requirements, know your customer (KYC) requirements, risk management and internal control (RMIC) requirements, financial reporting requirements (FRR), and consumer protection requirements (CPR) on fraud detection capabilities. Using a cross-sectional survey design, data were collected from 214 compliance officers, internal auditors, and risk managers across 14 listed deposit money banks in Nigeria through a structured questionnaire administered via Google Forms. The study employed descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation analysis, and multiple regression analysis using SPSS version 28.0 to analyze the data. The findings revealed that all five regulatory requirements have significant positive effects on financial fraud detection among Nigerian banks. Risk management and internal control requirements demonstrated the strongest effect (β=0.356, p<0.05), followed by consumer protection requirements (β=0.287, p<0.05), know your customer requirements (β=0.198, p<0.05), anti-money laundering requirements (β=0.142, p<0.05), and financial reporting requirements (β=0.124, p<0.05). The regression model explained 72.1% of the variance in fraud detection (R²=0.721), indicating a very good model fit. All null hypotheses were rejected, confirming that each regulatory requirement significantly enhances fraud detection capabilities. The study concludes that regulatory requirements play a crucial role in enhancing fraud detection among Nigerian deposit money banks, with risk management and consumer protection measures being particularly important. The findings suggest that banks should adopt a holistic approach to regulatory compliance, prioritizing risk management frameworks while strengthening consumer protection mechanisms to optimize fraud detection effectiveness.
