title: Environmental, social and governance reporting, audit committee characteristics and readability of annual reports: evidence from an African emerging economy
summary: Purpose The study examined the moderating effect of audit committee characteristics in the nexus between environmental, social and governance (ESG) reporting and annual report readability. Design/methodology/approach The study used archival data from the audited annual reports of 30 firms listed on the Ghana Stock Exchange, spanning the period 2000–2023. A fixed-effects estimator was employed, helping to address the potential issue of unobserved firm-specific heterogeneity in the dataset. However, system GMM was also used for robustness testing and to minimise issues that come with endogeneity as far as econometric estimates are concerned. Findings The result revealed that although ESG reporting could impair the readability of annual reports, in the presence of audit committee characteristics, namely audit committee size, audit committee gender diversity and audit committee meetings, ESG reporting could enhance readability (i.e. understandability) of annual reports. Practical implications While firms may want to ensure accountability and transparency to their numerous stakeholders by way of ESG reporting, it is imperative they do so, having an effective audit committee in place. This can be achieved by way of ensuring a larger audit committee that is gender diversified, but must be cautious in terms of engaging in more meetings. Originality/value The study adds to extant literature on ESG reporting and governance by showing that while ESG reporting may be important, it may impair the readability of annual reports, but the audit committee and its associated features, particularly gender diversity and bigger-size audit committee, can ensure more readable annual reports even in the presence of increasing ESG reporting.

title: CSR investments and innovation - Aligning and creating shared value: A critical review
summary: Purpose – This study critically evaluates the theoretical foundations, construct operationalization, methodological rigor, and empirical validity of the study CSR investments and innovation – Aligning and creating shared value. The review focuses on how external environmental responsibility, internal employee-focused social responsibility, and ethical governance responsibility are linked to CSR investments and subsequent product, service, and process innovations, as well as whether the proposed relationships are adequately supported by the research design and measurement procedures. Design/methodology/approach – This research employs a critical literature review methodology to systematically assess the theoretical foundations, methodological robustness, construct measurement, sampling strategy, statistical procedures, and contextual boundaries of the reviewed study. Particular attention is given to the cross-sectional sample of 410 organizations, the use of covariance-based structural equation modelling (SEM), multi-group comparisons across organizational sizes, the operationalization of CSR investments and innovation, the pooling of private, public, and not-for-profit organizations, and the use of Exploratory Factor Analysis and Confirmatory Factor Analysis. Findings – The review identifies several important conceptual, psychometric, and methodological vulnerabilities. The operationalization of the core constructs presents tautological overlap between the exogenous CSR dimensions and the mediating CSR investments construct, while the empirical measurement of innovation does not fully reflect the theoretical emphasis on innovation aligned with shared value. The pooling of private, public, not-for-profit, sole trader, and partnership organizations also creates substantial sectoral heterogeneity that may weaken the internal validity of the structural relationships. Furthermore, the single-informant cross-sectional design creates potential risks of common method variance, simultaneity bias, and reverse causality. The use of Exploratory Factor Analysis with Varimax rotation followed by Confirmatory Factor Analysis on the same sample also raises concerns regarding psychometric redundancy, overfitting, and the appropriateness of the measurement validation procedure. Originality/value – This study provides a critical perspective on the empirical examination of the CSR–investment–innovation relationship by identifying methodological and conceptual tensions that may affect the robustness of the reported findings. The review highlights the importance of clearer construct differentiation, stronger alignment between theoretical concepts and their empirical measures, more homogeneous sampling strategies, longitudinal research designs, and independent validation procedures. These considerations provide directions for future research examining how CSR practices and investments contribute to innovation and shared value creation across organizational contexts. title: Кутубхона фаолиятини модернизация қилиш: хорижий тажриба ва қиёсий таҳлил
summary: This article provides a comprehensive analysis of the sociological and institutional foundations for modernizing the activities of information-library institutions based on foreign experience. Specifically, it comparatively examines the activities of national and educational libraries in developed countries such as the USA, Germany, France, Japan, and South Korea, along with their legal frameworks and management models. Furthermore, scientific and practical proposals are developed to transform libraries from traditional book depositories into innovative centers that drive the digital transformation of society and foster media literacy and social communication. The conclusions presented in the article hold significant methodological importance for improving the national information-library system and developing its digital ecosystem.

title: Between opportunity and uncertainty: Mining employees’ perceptions of the Fourth Industrial Revolution
summary: Orientation: Digitalisation and automation associated with the Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR) have improved productivity, safety and sustainability in mining, but have also raised concerns about job security, skills mismatches and workforce readiness. Research purpose: This study explored employees’ perceptions of the impact of 4IR on the South African mining industry, focusing on workforce dynamics, operational processes, regulatory implications, and the challenges and opportunities arising from technological transformation. Motivation for the study: Although 4IR technologies can strengthen operational efficiency and competitiveness, they may also intensify concerns about job displacement and skills shortages. Understanding employees’ perceptions is therefore essential for sustainable digital transformation and workforce resilience. Research approach/design and method: A qualitative approach involved semi-structured interviews with 12 employees from a South African mining organisation selected through convenience sampling. Data were examined using inductive content analysis. Main findings: Adaptation to 4IR was shaped by individual adaptability resources, namely concern, control, curiosity and confidence, and organisational factors such as training quality, effective communication and participative change management. Inconsistent reskilling and limited psychological support reduced employee readiness and confidence. Practical/managerial implications: Mining organisations should adopt human-centred automation strategies supported by continuous reskilling, transparent communication, psychological support and structured, participative change management. Contribution/value-add: The study extends limited empirical knowledge of employee-centred digital transformation in mining and offers guidance to policymakers and industry leaders seeking to balance technological advancement with workforce sustainability.

title: Fuzzy MICMAC-Based Study of Barriers to Industry 4.0 and Lean Six Sigma Integration in Indian Smart Manufacturing
summary: ABSTRACT The integration of Industry 4.0 (I4.0) technologies with Lean Six Sigma (LSS) has emerged as a promising approach for enhancing operational efficiency, flexibility, and resilience in modern manufacturing systems. Despite its potential benefits, organizations continue to encounter multiple interrelated barriers that impede successful implementation. This study aims to identify and analyze the key barriers affecting the integration of I4.0 and LSS in Indian manufacturing organizations. A structured literature review followed by a two-round Delphi-based expert validation was conducted to identify and refine fifteen key barriers. The fuzzy Cross-Impact Matrix Multiplication applied to Classification method was subsequently employed to analyze the structural relationships among these barriers using triangular fuzzy numbers to capture uncertainty in expert judgments. The results classified the identified barriers into two categories, namely linkage barriers and autonomous barriers, based on their driving and dependence power. The most influential linkage barriers include high implementation cost, lack of skilled workforce, inadequate top management commitment, poor data quality and availability, integration issues with legacy systems, limited cross-functional collaboration, and vendor or partner limitations. The findings highlight the importance of workforce capability development, leadership commitment, technological readiness, and organizational collaboration in achieving successful digital transformation. The study offers a structured basis for prioritizing managerial interventions, supporting strategic decision-making, and planning technology adoption in manufacturing organizations. Although the findings are based on expert judgments within the Indian manufacturing context and should therefore be generalized with appropriate caution, the proposed framework provides a useful foundation for future research. Subsequent studies may validate the framework across different industrial sectors and geographical contexts, integrate hybrid multi-criteria decision-making techniques, and examine how implementation barriers can be transformed into organizational enablers for digital transformation.

title: ADVANTAGES AND THREATS OF GLOBALIZATION AND THE USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN MODERN MANAGEMENT
summary: This article examines the impact of globalization and artificial intelligence technologies on the development of modern business management in the context of the economy’s digital transformation. It argues that the digitalization of business, the development of information and communication technologies, the proliferation of big data, cloud services, intelligent analytics, and generative artificial intelligence are significantly changing approaches to enterprise management, facilitating the automation of business processes, improving the effectiveness of managerial decisionmaking, and strengthening the competitiveness of economic entities. It has been determined that globalization processes create new opportunities for the integration of enterprises into the global economic space, the development of international cooperation, and the expansion of access to innovative technologies and digital platforms, but at the same time give rise to new risks related to cybersecurity, information security, ethical aspects of artificial intelligence use, algorithmic bias, and growing dependence on digital infrastructure. The aim of this study is to conduct a comprehensive analysis of the benefits and threats posed by globalization processes and the use of artificial intelligence technologies in modern management, as well as to identify the main directions for their effective use to improve the performance of enterprises. The study employed methods of scientific generalization, systematic analysis, comparison, structural-logical analysis, and graphical modeling, which made it possible to comprehensively assess the impact of digital transformation on management functions. The article systematizes the key advantages and potential threats of using artificial intelligence in business operations and summarizes the main areas of its implementation in human resources management, marketing, logistics, finance, and strategic management. The authors have developed their own conclusions regarding the impact of globalization processes and artificial intelligence technologies on the core functions of enterprise management, specifically planning, organization, motivation, control, coordination, leadership, and innovation. It has been established that the effectiveness of artificial intelligence use directly depends on a company’s level of digital maturity, the availability of modern digital infrastructure, the development of staff digital competencies, and the implementation of effective information security management mechanisms. The practical significance of these findings lies in the ability of enterprise managers to use the proposed recommendations when formulating a digital development strategy, implementing artificial intelligence technologies, improving business process management systems, minimizing digital risks, and ensuring the sustainable development of enterprises in the context of globalization.

title: Measuring digital payment transformation in small retail businesses: mixed-method evidence from blockchain adoption in Colombia
summary: Abstract This study aims to evaluate how blockchain-based payment systems affect operational performance, customer-related outcomes, and organizational coordination in small retail businesses operating under institutional fragmentation and uneven digital infrastructure. Using transaction-level data from 76 small retailers in Colombia’s Caribbean region, the analysis combines pre/post comparisons, non-parametric tests, repeated-measures models, regression controls, endogeneity checks, and thematic content analysis of open-ended pre- and post-implementation questionnaire responses from participating business owners or managers. The findings show improvements in transaction speed, payment reliability, operating costs, customer retention, and perceived service quality, but they also reveal that these effects are conditioned by infrastructure quality, staff readiness, seasonality, and local market composition. Rather than treating blockchain as an isolated technological intervention, the study interprets payment adoption as a socio-technical governance mechanism that reorganizes coordination, trust, and operational routines. The article contributes to digital transformation research by offering a mixed-method framework for evaluating technology adoption in small firms where causal inference is constrained by non-random adoption, heterogeneous contexts, and imperfect administrative records.

title: Who Is Responsible When AI Shapes Corporate Decisions? Director Duties and Corporate Accountability under Indian Company Law
summary: A company is deciding whether to acquire another business. An artificial intelligence system examines financial records, market data and compliance risks, and recommends that the deal should proceed. The directors approve it. Months later, the acquisition causes serious loss. The board signed the resolution, but the model shaped the information and the choice. Who was really responsible? This article examines that question through section 166 of the Companies Act, 2013. It argues that directors may use AI, just as they use lawyers, auditors and other advisers, but they must not allow assistance to become substituted judgment. The relevant legal question is not whether the model was perfect. It is whether the directors understood its purpose, considered its limits, questioned important assumptions and retained the practical ability to reject its recommendation. The article distinguishes routine assistance, decision support and decision substitution. It then explains how opacity, automation bias, defective data and fragmented vendor arrangements may weaken accountability. Drawing on Indian company law and comparative principles reflected in the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act and Indian financial regulation, the article proposes five safeguards: disclosure of material AI use, board-level competence, governance-level explanation, records and continuing model review, and non-delegable human responsibility. Corporate governance may become algorithmically informed, but it cannot become algorithmically unaccountable.

title: Circular logistics as part of the supply chain
summary: This paper investigates circular logistics and its impact on the efficiency and sustainability of the supply chain. Key trends from 2019 to 2024 are analyzed, including the adoption of advanced technologies such as Blockchain, the Internet of Things (IoT), and artificial intelligence (AI), as well as recycling and material reuse, simplified product returns, and sustainable packaging. A qualitative analysis of secondary data, including scholarly articles and company reports, shows that the implementation of circular logistics reduces operational costs and waste, while its success depends on developed recycling infrastructure and the adaptation of business models. The study connects circular economy theory with practical examples, provides insights into the challenges and success factors in integrating circular models into supply chains, and offers guidance for future research and practical application.

title: DIGITAL MATURITY AS A FACTOR IN THE DEVELOPMENT OF THE TOURISM AND RECREATIONAL SPHERE
summary: In today's world, digital transformation has become an integral part of the competitiveness development in almost all economy sectors. The tourism and recreation industry are no exception, as it is one of the most dynamic and sensitive sectors to the ongoing economy and consumer behavior transformation. This article explores the concept of «digital maturity», which reflects the industry's ability to adapt to new challenges, improve resource efficiency, and create innovative value propositions for consumers. The «digital maturity» concept in this context means not just the individual technological solutions implementation, but a comprehensive transformation of business processes and management models, as well as the customer experience based on digital tools. The paper identifies four key components of a destination's digital maturity. To verify the hypothesis about the impact of digital maturity on the tourism and recreation sector development, the paper uses data from Rosstat.

title: Changing Patterns of Consumer Buying Behavior in the Digital Era: A Study of Nagpur District
summary: The rapid advancement of digital technologies has significantly transformed consumer buying behavior across the globe.This study investigates the changing patterns of consumer buying behavior in the digital era with special reference to Nagpur district.The research adopts a descriptive and analytical approach using primary data collected from 100 respondents through a structured questionnaire.Statistical tools such as percentage analysis and the Chi-square test were applied to examine the relationship between digital factors and consumer purchasing decisions.The findings reveal that online platforms, social media, and convenience play a crucial role in shaping modern consumer behavior.The study concludes that digital transformation has made consumers more informed, value-conscious, and technology-driven.The research provides important implications for marketers, businesses, and policymakers.

title: Bibliometric Study of the Intersection Between Green Energy and Artificial Intelligence: Business- and Economy-Related Studies
summary: The rapid convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and green energy (GE) is transforming sustainable business practices, energy management, and economic development. Although research in this interdisciplinary field has expanded considerably, its intellectual structure, thematic evolution, and business implications remain insufficiently understood. This study presents a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of AI and GE research from a business and economics perspective. Publications were retrieved from the Scopus and Web of Science databases using an expanded, transparent, and reproducible search strategy. Following PRISMA guidelines and predefined inclusion criteria, a final dataset of 7,301 publications was analyzed using Bibliometrix and VOSviewer to examine publication trends, influential authors, institutions, countries, journals, collaboration networks, and thematic structures. The results reveal a marked increase in scientific production after 2022, reflecting the growing integration of AI into renewable energy systems and sustainable development research. Scientific output is concentrated in countries with strong research capacity, sustained investment in digital innovation, and ambitious sustainability agendas. Keyword co-occurrence analysis identifies four dominant research themes: sustainability and energy policy, AI-driven forecasting and optimization, smart energy systems, and digital transformation for energy efficiency. The findings demonstrate that the field has evolved from predominantly technical applications toward a multidisciplinary research domain integrating business strategy, innovation management, sustainability, and energy economics. Unlike previous bibliometric studies based on narrower search strategies or smaller datasets, this study provides a transparent, large-scale mapping of the field and offers a more comprehensive understanding of its intellectual structure and emerging research directions. The findings provide valuable insights for researchers, policymakers, managers, and investors seeking to accelerate sustainable energy transitions and support long-term economic resilience.

title: Corporate Governance Mechanisms, Managerial Ability and Financial Performance in the Nigerian Banking Industry
summary: Good corporate governance has become a vital ingredient for financial stability in the banking industry, especially in developing economies where weak institutional structures often undermine performance. This study examined how corporate governance mechanisms shape the financial performance of Nigerian deposit money banks, with particular attention to the mediating role of managerial ability. The specific objectives were to analyse the effect of corporate governance mechanisms on financial performance; to investigate how corporate governance influences managerial ability, and to assess the effect of managerial ability on financial performance. The study adopted a quantitative, explanatory design, using panel data from twelve purposively sampled Nigerian deposit money banks listed on the Nigerian Exchange, covering 2012–2023 (144 bank-year observations). Corporate governance was proxied by board size, expertise, gender diversity, independence and audit committee size; managerial ability was estimated via stochastic frontier analysis (Demerjian et al., 2012); and financial performance was measured with return on equity (ROE). Panel regression (pooled OLS, fixed and random effects, selected via Breusch–Pagan LM and Hausman tests) was employed, controlling for bank size and leverage. Findings show that, individually, governance mechanisms had no statistically significant direct effect on financial performance or managerial ability. Managerial ability, however, had a positive and highly significant effect on financial performance, confirming its mediating role. The study concludes that governance structures alone cannot guarantee profitability unless backed by competent managers and recommends that banks and regulators move beyond compliance-based governance toward board engagement quality and leadership development.

title: Artificial Intelligence, Green Innovation and Organizational Learning in Pakistan
summary: The development of artificial intelligence and environmental innovations is changing the processes of knowledge management, decision‑making, and organizational learning in companies in the digital sector. The aim of the study is to assess the impact of implementing artificial intelligence and green innovations on organizational learning, taking into account the mediating role of decision‑making quality and knowledge management potential, as well as the moderating role of digital infrastructure in the information and communication technology sector in Pakistan. The study uses a quantitative approach and a cross‑sectional survey method. The initial data were obtained based on a questionnaire survey of 300 employees of companies in the information and communication sector in Lahore, Pakistan. The results demonstrated a positive impact of artificial intelligence implementation on organizational learning (β=0.650; t=5.520; p<0.001) and green innovations on organizational learning (β=0.400; t=3.921; p=0.002). The quality of decision‑making (β = 0.504; t = 4.134; p = 0.008) and knowledge management potential (β = 0.555; t = 5.428; p < 0.001) are also positively associated with organizational learning. Digital infrastructure strengthens the link between the implementation of artificial intelligence and organizational learning (β=0.220; t=2.45; p=0.031), as well as between green innovations and organizational learning (β=0.318; t=3.29; p=0.001). The results obtained are of social significance, as the development of artificial intelligence, green innovations, and digital infrastructure contributes to improving knowledge exchange, collaborative learning and the adaptability of employees in organizations.

title: MAKING TUIT THE HUB OF INFORMATION SCIENCE EDUCATION IN CIS COUNTRIES: STRATEGIES, REQUIREMENTS, AND FUTURE HORIZONS
summary: The accelerating digital transformation across the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) highlights the urgent need for a regional leader in information science education. This paper argues that the Tashkent University of Information Technologies (TUIT) is uniquely positioned to serve as the hub for advancing curricula, research, and innovation in the field. Using a qualitative review of global higher education trends, regional challenges, and hub university models, the paper identifies strategies for TUIT to strengthen its leadership role. Key strategies include curriculum modernization, faculty development, digital infrastructure enhancement, regional collaboration, and student mobility initiatives. The study also outlines the requirements necessary to implement these strategies, including sustainable funding, supportive policies, human capital development, and strong academic networks. Looking ahead, the paper envisions TUIT evolving into a regional center of excellence that drives digital innovation, fosters international collaboration, and advances social inclusion. The findings suggest that establishing TUIT as a hub is not only feasible but also critical for building a competitive and interconnected knowledge economy in the CIS

title: Digital Fatigue in the Digital Workplace: Emerging Occupational Risks and the Georgian Context
summary: Along with substantial benefits, digital transformation has increased reliance on digital communication, continuous connectivity and screen-based work, raising concerns about digital fatigue, digital overload and technostress. This narrative review examines digital fatigue, its relationship to related digital stressors, work-related and health consequences, and approaches to its management, with particular attention to Georgia. Recent peer-reviewed research and publications of international and national institutions were considered. The review indicates that digital fatigue is an emerging construct rather than an established medical diagnosis or occupational disease. Recent studies report associations with adverse work-related outcomes, including lower work engagement and job performance, although evidence remains limited and concentrated in specific occupational populations. Factors associated with digital fatigue and its reported outcomes overlap with recognised occupational psychosocial risks, including digital overload and blurred work–life boundaries. Responses increasingly address these risks through organisational practices, psychosocial-risk management and working-time arrangements, alongside individual approaches such as digital detox. In Georgia, digital connectivity has expanded substantially, but evidence on the occupational consequences of intensive digital technology use remains limited. The review highlights the need for research linking digital demands with digital fatigue and technostress, symptoms, work engagement and performance, absenteeism. Where feasible, it link these findings to productivity indicators and subsequent estimates of economic costs.

title: Strategic Optimization of Industrial Lubricants for Energy Efficiency and Asset Reliability in Saudi Arabia’s Oil and Gas Sector: A Vision 2030 Framework
summary: Industrial lubrication is usually regarded as a maintenance item rather than as a means of achieving energy efficiency, asset reliability, and lifecycle value. This difference is important in Saudi Arabia's oil and gas industry, since pumps, compressors, turbines, gearboxes, hydraulic systems and auxiliary equipment have to operate under heavy loads, thermal stress, a risk of contamination and strict availability requirements. This study brings together peer-reviewed evidence published between 2020 and 2025 in order to look at how lubricant selection, application engineering, contamination control, condition monitoring, predictive analytics and sustainable formulation can be incorporated into a strategic lubrication framework that is in line with Saudi Vision 2030. To do this, a structured integrative approach is applied drawing on the fields of tribology, reliability engineering, condition monitoring, digital transformation and the literature on Saudi energy transition. The evidence shows that lubricant optimisation improves efficiency by reducing friction and churning losses, enhances reliability by ensuring good film integrity and controlling wear, and has an impact on maintenance costs by enabling earlier detection of degradation and allowing for better timing of interventions. Yet value is sacrificed when lubricant decisions are left scattered among the procurement, operations, laboratories and maintenance departments. It is therefore suggested that a framework geared towards Saudi Vision 2030 should be based on five interconnected capabilities: asset criticality, application-specific lubricant engineering, condition-based surveillance, data-driven decision support, and circular resource management. The review concludes that the greatest opportunity does not lie in simply using higher-performance oils, but in treating lubrication as an asset-management system that delivers measurable results in the areas of energy, reliability, environment and localisation.

title: SUSTAINABILITY AND DIGITALIZATION INITIATIVES AMONG YOUNG MICRO-ENTREPRENEURS IN BATAAN: BASIS FOR PROPOSED BUSINESS STRATEGIC FRAMEWORK
summary: Continuous industrialization and rapid digital transformation have significantly changed economic activity and human well-being. Industrial Revolution 5.0, characterized by integrating technology with human values, calls for promoting young entrepreneurs to build businesses that are sustainable, socially responsible, and capable of contributing to inclusive economic growth by supporting the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals. This study examined sustainability practices across environmental, social, and economic dimensions; assessed digital adoption through digital awareness, technology, people, products or services, and business processes. The study also explored the experiences and challenges encountered in implementing sustainability practices and adopting digital technologies. The study used a mixed-methods approach, including survey responses from 88 young micro-entrepreneurs and in-depth interview with 22 participants. This study was completed during the Academic Year 2025-2026. The findings reveal a gap between awareness and strategic implementation. Sustainability efforts focus more on internal practices, while digitalization focuses on daily operational efficiency and external reach. Altogether, sustainability and digital integration remain in their early stages. To address this, the study proposes a business strategic framework that supports the progression from survival-oriented operations toward more integrated practices.

title: Challenges and Benefits of Implementing Smart Hospital Systems in Specialized Orthopedic Centers: A Systematic Review
summary: The increasing complexity of healthcare services has encouraged specialized orthopedic centers to adopt smart hospital systems as an approach to improve service integration, operational efficiency, and patient-centered care. However, the implementation of these systems remains challenging due to technological, organizational, financial, and human resource limitations. This study aims to explore the benefits and challenges of implementing smart hospital systems in specialized orthopedic centers by examining their contributions to healthcare performance, operational processes, and patient experience. This research employed a systematic literature review approach by analyzing relevant studies related to smart hospitals, digital transformation, artificial intelligence, hospital information systems, and orthopedic healthcare services. A total of 25 studies were selected through a PRISMA-based screening process from an initial 200 identified records. The findings indicate that smart hospital systems provide significant benefits, including improved workflow coordination, faster access to medical information, enhanced clinical decision-making, increased surgical precision through advanced technologies, and improved continuity of rehabilitation care. Nevertheless, several challenges were identified, including limited infrastructure, high implementation costs, interoperability issues, data reliability concerns, and the need for user adaptation and training. In conclusion, smart hospital systems support more efficient, integrated, and patient-oriented orthopedic healthcare services; however, successful implementation requires technological readiness, organizational commitment, and continuous improvement strategies.

title: Does competitive advantage strengthen the value relevance of ESG disclosure?
summary: Type of the article: Research ArticleIn the evolving landscape of ASEAN capital markets, environmental, social, and governance (ESG) disclosure is increasingly recognized as a strategic driver of corporate value, with competitive advantage determining the extent to which its benefits are realized. This study aims to examine how competitive advantage moderates the relationship between ESG disclosure and firm value in the ASEAN emergent context. The study applies panel data comprising 2,801 observations from 726 listed companies in ASEAN during 2015-2023. Regression analysis was conducted using the two-step System Generalized Method of Moments, accompanied by a series of robustness tests. The findings emphasize ESG reporting benefits, as ESG disclosure positively influences all firm value proxies in baseline models (βESG_Tobin’sQ = 0.0034, p-value < 0.05; βESG_LogMC = 0.0040, p-value < 0.01; βESG_PB = 0.0047, p-value < 0.05). The interaction between ESG disclosure and competitive advantage is also positive and significant across the three measures (βESGxCA_Tobin’sQ = 0.0545, p-value < 0.05; βESGxCA_LogMC = 0.0254, p-value < 0.01; βESGxCA_PB = 0.0678, p-value < 0.01). These results suggest that the valuation implications of ESG disclosure are contingent on firms’ competitive advantage, with the estimated marginal effect generally increasing as competitive advantage improves. Accordingly, the study enriches the literature by resonating with the intersection between stakeholder theory and the resource-based view (RBV), demonstrating how competitive advantage conditions the link between ESG disclosure and firm value in ASEAN capital markets. The study suggests that managers should align financial objectives with stakeholder expectations and integrate ESG disclosure into broader corporate strategies to enhance valuation purposes.

title: Digital innovation enablers in sustainable banking and insurance: a systematic review of business model transformation factors
summary: Banking and insurance institutions face increasing pressure to transform their business models through digital technologies while advancing sustainability objectives, yet existing research remains fragmented in explaining how digital innovation is translated into sustainable outcomes. This systematic review applies PRISMA guidelines to synthesize 168 peer-reviewed articles published between 2002 and 2026 from Scopus and Web of Science, using systematic screening, structured coding, and thematic analysis to examine the links among digital transformation, business model innovation, and sustainable performance in banking and insurance. The review identifies an evolutionary trajectory from basic digitalization and financial inclusion models toward AI-enabled, ecosystem-based, and sustainability-integrated business model transformation. More importantly, the synthesis develops a mechanism-based explanation of sustainable transformation by showing that business model innovation functions as an enabler, amplifier, mediator, moderator, and boundary spanner through five mechanisms: technology-enabled inclusion, ecosystem orchestration, revenue model transformation, risk resilience engineering, and stakeholder value co-creation. The review further proposes a four-archetype framework comprising The Reinventors, The Mavericks, The Adapters, and The Adventurers, each reflecting different combinations of innovation impetus, organizational focus, sectoral logic, and sustainability orientation. By translating these findings into concrete and testable propositions, this review contributes a parsimonious research agenda for examining when, how, and under what conditions digital business model innovation produces sustainable transformation in banking and insurance.

title: Effect of Audit Firm Size on Audit Fees of Listed Agricultural Firms in Nigeria
summary: This study ascertained the effect of audit firm size on audit fees of listed agricultural firms in Nigeria. The study adopted an ex-post facto, quantitative research design, and drew its data from the published audited annual reports and accounts of the five companies that constitute the entire population of firms listed under the agricultural sector of the Nigerian Exchange Group. The study found that audit firm size has a positive and statistically significant effect on audit fees (β = 1.5602), significant under conventional standard errors (p = 0.0018) and, if anything, more strongly significant under cluster-robust standard errors (p = 0.0003), the single most robust finding of the study, leading to the rejection of the null hypothesis. Firms audited by Big Four audit firms were found to pay significantly higher audit fees than firms audited by non-Big four firms, holding other factors constant. The study thus recommended that the Financial Reporting Council of Nigeria and the Nigerian Exchange Group should consider strengthening the requirement for listed companies to disclose audit fees clearly and consistently as a distinct line item in the notes to their financial statements, to support both external monitoring of auditor independence.

title: Digital competency and ICT leadership in rural basic-education schools in Northeastern Thailand: A needs analysis informing an adaptive digital support system
summary: This study addresses the lack of context-specific evidence on digital transformation in basic education. It investigates the digital competency, ICT use, and ICT leadership readiness of 192 teachers and 111 school administrators (N = 303) in opportunity-expansion schools — state-supported rural schools serving lower-secondary grades — across five provinces of Northeastern Thailand. A descriptive survey, complemented by semi-structured interviews with 12 experts, examined school infrastructure, digital access and use, self-assessed competencies, and priority needs. Developmental needs were quantified using the modified Priority Needs Index ( P N I modified ), and interviews were thematically analysed to triangulate the findings. Both groups used digital tools across administration, teaching, assessment, and professional learning, yet outdated and insufficient hardware remained the principal constraint. Current competency was rated moderately high to high, while desired levels were consistently higher, producing modest but systematic gaps. The highest relative needs were concentrated among administrators, in basic digital operations ( P N I modified = 0.104) and community and network engagement ( P N I modified = 0.074), followed by teachers' basic digital operations and digital assessment — indicating a challenge of quality and depth rather than of access. Administrators rated themselves slightly higher than teachers overall, with small-to-moderate effect sizes. These findings informed a conceptually designed Adaptive Digital Support System (ADSS) with three modules — user profiling, resource alignment, and progress monitoring — specified conceptually and not empirically evaluated. The findings offer practical and theoretical insights for strengthening digital capacity in comparable resource-constrained contexts.

title: Evaluating the Sustainability of a Corporate Social Responsibility Program in Women's Empowerment: A CIPP Model Analysis of the Dadi Juara SMEs Sewing Program
summary: This study evaluates the Dadi Juara Sewing MSME Program of PT Pertamina Patra Niaga Integrated Terminal Surabaya, an empowerment initiative for Socially and Economically Vulnerable Women (PRSE) in Tanjung Perak Subdistrict, Pabean Cantian District, Surabaya City. Using Participatory Action Research (PAR) as its methodology, the study applies the Context, Input, Process, Product (CIPP) evaluation model to assess the program's alignment with community needs, planning, implementation, and outcomes after three years. The context evaluation shows that the program responds to women's unequal access to the formal labor market, skill gaps among PRSE, and regulatory obligations under PERMEN LH/BPLH Number 7 of 2025. The input evaluation indicates that the selected strategy is more appropriate than alternative strategies, although no explicit exit strategy has been formulated. The process evaluation reveals a gap between the support and the group's substantive capacity, marked by stagnant membership, sewing orders limited to low-value alterations, and the absence of a formal memorandum of understanding with business partners. The product evaluation shows that achievements remain dominated by outputs, while substantive independence has not been fully achieved. The study recommends strengthening institutional capacity, standardizing product quality, and expanding market access to achieve sustainable economic independence.

title: Corporate governance and HR ethics: case insights on compliance programs
summary: Abstract This study examines how compliance programs operate as governance mechanisms, shaping the ethical conduct of human resources over time. Drawing on Michel Foucault’s conceptualization of ethics, the paper analyses how different configurations of compliance practices influence employees’ moral subjectification. The study adopts a qualitative case study approach, based on 19 semi-structured interviews with organizational members holding governance, leadership, and operational roles in a pharmaceutical company operating under the Italian Legislative Decree (LD) 231/01, complemented by documentary analysis. The findings reveal a two-stage process. In the initial phase, the compliance program functioned primarily through the technologies of government, emphasizing control, monitoring, and sanctions. These mechanisms constrained employees’ discretion and fostered compliance, driven by fear of punishment rather than ethical engagement. In the subsequent phase, changes in leadership practices—particularly the role of the Compliance Officer—reoriented the compliance program toward enabling technologies that supported ethical reflection, autonomy, and self-regulation. As a result, employees increasingly perceived compliance as a resource for responsible decision-making rather than a coercive constraint. The study contributes to the governance literature by showing how the same compliance framework can produce different ethical outcomes, depending on how governance mechanisms are enacted and interpreted. This highlights the critical role of leadership in aligning control systems with the development of ethical self-governance.

title: Leading with happiness in AI-driven transformation: a qualitative study of happiness-based leadership and employee well-being
summary: Purpose The study aims to examine how leaders who explicitly embrace happiness and well-being as core values practice leadership during the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI). It investigates how such happiness-based leaders interpret and enact their roles and how employees experience these practices in terms of motivation, trust, psychological safety and mental health. Design/methodology/approach Adopting a qualitative, interpretivist design grounded in abductive logic, the study draws on narrative interviews with top, middle and frontline leaders, complemented by semi-structured interviews and focus groups with employees across four organizations undergoing active AI implementation. Observations of town halls, change workshops and team interactions further inform the analysis. Combining narrative and thematic analysis enables interpretation of both leaders’ meaning-making stories and their enacted micro-practices in daily AI-related work contexts. Findings The study develops the concept of happiness-based digital leadership as a multidimensional configuration of practices comprising: (1) meaning-framing of AI, linking technology to organizational purpose and human values; (2) emotional containment, acknowledging fear and fatigue while modelling realistic optimism; (3) inclusive involvement, embedding participation and ethical safeguards in AI-related decisions; and (4) boundary work, protecting time, workload and human decision zones within AI governance. Three distinct leadership regimes – deep, rhetorical and instrumental – are identified, differing in the degree to which happiness practices are authentically integrated into AI governance or deployed as compliance mechanisms. Deep happiness-based digital leadership sustains trust, psychological safety and well-being; rhetorical and instrumental regimes risk turning happiness discourse into a soft form of technocratic control. Originality/value This research extends happiness management and positive leadership scholarship into AI-intensive contexts, explicating how happiness management principles can be enacted at the leadership level in AI governance. It offers conceptual and empirical insights into the emotional, ethical and governance dimensions of digital transformation, introduces a theoretically grounded typology of happiness-based leadership regimes and enriches understanding of psychological safety and emotional climate during technological change.

title: Pengaruh Keuangan Berkelanjutan terhadap Nilai Perusahaan dengan Profitabilitas Sebagai Variabel Mediasi pada Sektor Perbankan di Bursa Efek Indonesia (BEI) 2020-2024
summary: Sustainable finance has become an important part of the banking sector's strategy as attention to environmental, social, and governance aspects increases in creating long-term corporate value. This study aims to analyze the influence of sustainable finance, as proxied by Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG), on firm value, analyze the influence of ESG on profitability and profitability on firm value, and examine the role of profitability as a mediating variable. The study uses a quantitative approach with secondary data sourced from annual reports, sustainability reports, and stock price data of banking companies listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange for the 2020–2024 period. The sample was determined using a purposive sampling technique, resulting in 10 companies with 50 observations. ESG disclosure was measured using content analysis based on 15 indicators adapted from the 2021 GRI Standards. Profitability was proxied by Return on Assets (ROA), while firm value was proxied by Price to Book Value (PBV). The analysis was conducted using Structural Equation Modeling–Partial Least Squares (SEM-PLS) with SmartPLS 4. The results showed that ESG has a positive and significant effect on firm value, but not a significant effect on profitability. Profitability has a positive and significant effect on firm value, but does not significantly mediate the relationship between ESG and firm value. These findings suggest that sustainable finance is associated with increased firm value primarily through the direct influence of ESG on market valuation, not through increased profitability.

title: Corporate Governance Reform and Organisational Accountability in Saudi Arabia: The Roles of Board Practices and Ownership Concentration
summary: This study examines how the post-reform corporate governance environment is associated with organisational accountability in Saudi Arabian listed firms and whether board practices represent potential pathways through which this association occurs in ownership-concentrated companies. A convergent mixed-methods design combines interviews with 28 governance actors and an unbalanced panel of 164 non-financial listed firms covering 2015 to 2024 (1476 firm-year observations). The qualitative and quantitative strands were conducted in parallel and integrated through a joint display that assessed convergence, complementarity, and tension across findings. The post-reform period is positively associated with organisational accountability, board independence, committee strength, and board gender diversity, while ownership concentration attenuates the reform-accountability association. Because the nationwide reform applied to listed firms concurrently and no untreated comparison group is available, the estimates are interpreted as conditional longitudinal associations rather than changes attributable specifically to regulation. Interview evidence indicates that stronger formal structures do not invariably correspond with behavioural independence or substantive scrutiny. The study contributes an institutional-translation account in which regulatory expectations acquire organisational meaning through board practices but remain conditioned by concentrated ownership and wider institutional change.

title: From Algorithmic Accuracy to Trusted Financial Integrity: A Theory-Building Systematic Review of Artificial Intelligence in Accounting, Auditing, and Fraud Detection
summary: Artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in accounting, auditing, and fraud-detection systems, yet existing research remains fragmented between studies emphasizing algorithmic performance and those examining professional, organizational, ethical, and regulatory conditions. This systematic literature review synthesizes 37 studies published between 2020 and 2025 and indexed in Scopus, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect to explain how, why, and under what conditions AI capability translates into trustworthy financial-control outcomes. Guided by PRISMA 2020 and a theory-building thematic synthesis, the review integrates evidence on machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, explainable AI, big data analytics, blockchain-enabled systems, and related digital technologies. The synthesis reveals that AI consistently strengthens transaction-level fraud detection, anomaly identification, audit analytics, and selected financial-reporting functions; however, technical performance alone does not ensure organizational effectiveness. Human professional capability, explainability, transparency, trust, cybersecurity maturity, organizational readiness, and regulatory governance emerge as critical mechanisms and boundary conditions. The evidence further reveals a digital fraud paradox in which the same technologies that strengthen detection may simultaneously increase the sophistication and adaptability of fraudulent behavior. Integrating Socio-Technical Systems Theory, the Technology–Organization–Environment framework, and responsible AI perspectives, this review develops a multi-level framework in which trusted financial integrity results from the alignment of technical capability, human judgment, responsible governance, and institutional readiness. The study advances the literature beyond algorithm comparison toward a conditional and socio-technical explanation of responsible AI-enabled financial control.

title: Does auditor industry specialization influence the relationship between financial statements comparability and audit effort? Egyptian evidence
summary: The joint influence of financial reporting attributes and auditor expertise on audit outcomes represents a central and underexplored nexus in the accounting and auditing literature. Building on Agency and Information Asymmetry theories, this study investigates the empirical relationship between financial statement comparability (FSC) and audit effort, as well as the moderating role of auditor industry specialization (AISPEC). Utilizing a balanced panel of 840 firm-year observations from 105 non-financial companies listed on the Egyptian Exchange (2017–2024), we estimate random effects panel regressions. Empirical findings indicate that FSC is significantly and negatively associated with audit effort. Crucially, AISPEC acts as a significant moderator, strengthening this negative link and indicating that the cost-reducing benefits of comparability are substantially more pronounced when audits are conducted by specialized firms. Extensive robustness checks including alternative comparability measures, an auditor concentration index, and Audit Report Lag consistently validate our baseline outcomes. Furthermore, addressing endogeneity through a Two-Step System Dynamic Panel GMM estimator confirms the causal reliability of our hypotheses. This study offers novel evidence from an emerging MENA economy, highlighting the critical operational synergy between financial reporting quality and specialized audit expertise.

title: IFRS 12 (Disclosure of Interests in Other Entities) and Financial Reporting Quality: Evidence from Listed Nigerian Companies
summary: Despite Nigeria's adoption of International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS), concerns persisted regarding the quality of corporate financial reporting due to inconsistent compliance with disclosure requirements, particularly those relating to interests in subsidiaries, associates, joint arrangements, and structured entities. This study examined the effect of IFRS 12 disclosure requirements on financial reporting quality among listed Nigerian companies. The study adopted an explanatory research design using secondary data obtained from selected non-financial companies listed on the Nigerian Exchange Group (NGX) between 2015 and 2024. An IFRS 12 Disclosure Compliance Index was employed to measure compliance, while financial reporting quality was assessed using the key qualitative characteristics of financial information. The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, and panel regression techniques. The findings revealed that disclosure of interests in subsidiaries had a positive and significant effect on transparency and accountability (β = 0.531, p = 0.000), disclosure of interests in associates had a negative and significant effect on information asymmetry (β = −0.418, p = 0.000), disclosure of interests in joint arrangements had a positive and significant effect on investor confidence (β = 0.467, p = 0.000), while disclosure of interests in structured entities had a positive and significant effect on financial reporting quality (β = 0.389, p = 0.000). Enhanced disclosures were found to improve transparency, reduce information asymmetry, strengthen corporate accountability, and increase investor confidence. The study concluded that the effective implementation of IFRS 12 contributed significantly to improved financial reporting quality in Nigeria. It was therefore recommended that regulatory enforcement should be strengthened, continuous professional training should be encouraged, and corporate governance practices should be enhanced to improve compliance and transparency.

title: The impact of market-incentive environmental policies on enterprise digital transformation: evidence from China’s carbon emissions trading pilot programmes
summary: Market-incentive environmental policies guide enterprises to proactively reduce emissions and undergo digital transformation by altering market signals and cost calculations, and are significant for the green economy. This study employs China’s carbon emissions trading pilot policy (Cpolicy) as a quasi-natural experiment. It uses a multi-period difference-in-differences (DID) model to analyze data on China’s A-share-listed enterprises (2010–2021). The results show that Cpolicy significantly drives enterprise digital transformation. This primarily stems from increases in goodwill, new investment, and innovation input and output triggered by Cpolicy. The effects of Cpolicy vary significantly across industries, firm sizes, and ownership types, underscoring the need for tailored policies. Furthermore, enterprise financial asset allocation and supply chain concentration show notable threshold effects; moderate levels of financial asset allocation and external collaboration enhance Cpolicy’s effectiveness. Overall, Cpolicy significantly stimulates enterprise digital transformation, but targeted measures are needed to maximise its impact.

title: AI-Assisted Audit Performance and Ethical Risk Governance in Financial Fraud Identification
summary: This study constructs a dual-cycle framework integrating financial fraud identification and ethical governance for artificial intelligence-assisted audit. It uses financial indicators, text features, and corporate governance variables to build multi-dimensional detection models. Traditional models and machine learning models including tree ensemble, explainable, and review-adjusted models are compared. Empirical results show that machine learning models outperform traditional models in fraud identification accuracy and stability. The explainable module and manual review can effectively reduce ethical risks such as opacity, bias amplification, over-reliance, and responsibility ambiguity. This work balances technical performance and ethical compliance, reveals ethical challenges of intelligent audit applications, and provides a governance path for the standardized application of artificial intelligence in auditing.

title: Earnings Management and Investment Opportunities in Frontier Markets: The Suppressor Role of Credit Risk
summary: This study examines the association between earnings management (EM) and investment opportunities through credit risk in a sanctioned frontier market. Using a balanced panel of 146 Tehran Stock Exchange firms (2018–2024) with Driscoll–Kraay standard errors and Wild Cluster Bootstrap, we find a positive direct association between EM and the investment opportunity set (IOS), consistent with reverse signaling that may reduce information asymmetry. EM is also positively associated with credit risk, which offsets approximately 17.43% of the direct effect, generating a risk–investment trade-off. The indirect pathway is modest and marginally significant, reflecting competitive mediation. Directional decomposition reveals that only income-increasing manipulation is positively linked to IOS, while income-decreasing manipulation is negatively associated with investment capacity. The results challenge the view of EM as purely opportunistic and highlight the need for adaptive, cash-flow-based credit assessment in frontier markets.

title: Building a Future-ready Governance Through Digital Transformation
summary: Governments are increasingly confronted with rapid technological change, artificial intelligence (AI), cybersecurity threats, demographic shifts, climate change, economic uncertainty, and evolving citizen expectations. These challenges require public institutions to move beyond traditional modernization approaches toward governance systems that are anticipatory, adaptive, agile, resilient, innovative, inclusive, citizen-centric, and data-driven. This study examines how digital transformation can contribute to building future-ready governments by identifying the institutional, technological, organizational, and human capabilities required to support sustainable public-sector transformation. The study employed a qualitative comparative research design using systematic document review and cross-country analysis. Countries with advanced digital government and digital transformation capabilities were identified through the United Nations E-Government Development Index (UN EGDI), the World Bank GovTech Maturity Index (GTMI), and the IMD World Digital Competitiveness Ranking (WDCR). The study subsequently examined selected international practices, with particular attention to the digital transformation strategies and governance approaches of Singapore, Denmark, and the Netherlands – having been ranked high in all 3 benchmarks (UN EGDI, GTMI and WDCR). The findings indicate that digital transformation is an important enabler of future-ready governance but is not, by itself, sufficient to achieve future readiness. The comparative analysis identified several interrelated dimensions that support future-ready government. Singapore demonstrates the value of trust, growth, community; AI, data, digital identity, seamless services, cybersecurity; Denmark highlights coherent services, cybersecurity, new technologies, digital inclusion, green transition; while the Netherlands emphasizes cloud, data, AI, citizen/business focus, digital resilience and autonomy, digital skills. The study concludes that building a future-ready government requires: (1) anticipatory governance and strategic foresight; (2) adaptive governance and agility; (3) institutional capacity and reform; (4) digitalized and data-driven governance; (5) human capabilities and digital skills; (6) innovation and continuous improvement; (7) resilience and cybersecurity; and (8) citizen-centered, inclusive and accountable governance – all of which cannot be addressed by digital transformation alone.

title: Quantifying the heterogeneous impacts of green innovation and renewable energy transition on climate pressure in Nigeria
summary: As countries intensify efforts to address climate change and advance sustainable development, understanding the effectiveness of green innovation and renewable energy transition in achieving climate goals has become increasingly important. Climate pressure is measured as the ecological footprint per capita, an indicator of the biologically productive land and sea area needed to support a population's consumption and absorb its waste. Previous research in this context, however, mostly employs mean-based estimators that do not account for potential conditional heterogeneity. This study investigates the distributional effects of green innovation and renewable energy transition on climate pressure in Nigeria. Green innovation is proxied by internet users as a share of the population, and renewable energy transition by the share of renewable electricity generation. The QARDL model is applied to annual data from 1990 to 2023, and the results show a stable long-run relationship between the variables. The findings also reveal strong heterogeneity in this relationship across the distribution of climate pressure. Green innovation and renewable energy sources are associated with a decrease in climate pressure in both the short and long run. Long-run elasticities range from - 0.087 at the tenth percentile to - 0.198 at the ninetieth percentile for green innovation, and from - 0.054 to - 0.141 for renewable energy. At higher climate pressure levels, the environmental gains of green innovation and renewable energy transition are significant. The Toda-Yamamoto causality test also suggests a unidirectional relationship from green innovation to climate pressure. Investment in digital infrastructure, clean technology and renewable energy deployment should therefore be prioritised. This is especially true during periods of high environmental stress, when climate benefits are highest. Such measures can make significant contributions toward climate and sustainable development goals in Nigeria. This is the first study to jointly estimate long-run, short-run, and error-correction dynamics across the full distribution of climate pressure for this nexus in a single African economy. The climate benefit of digital and renewable investment is shown to roughly double in strength exactly when environmental pressure is most severe.

title: Empirical research on organizational learning capability enhancing resilience performance in digital transformation
summary: Digital transformation opens up more opportunities for organizational access to information, automation, and platform-enabled coordination, but it also creates risks of exposure to the unpredictability of technology and dependency on others. The present study tests if organizational learning capacity enhances organizational resilience performance directly and indirectly through digital adaptive capacity. Cross-sectional survey methodology is defined for a sample of 420 middle and senior managers from Chinese manufacturing and service firms which have been undergoing enterprise-wide digital transformation for at least two years. Organizational learning capacity is conceptualized as a second-order latent variable made up of knowledge acquisition, knowledge sharing, experimentation, and reflective learning. Partial least squares structural equation modeling with 5,000 bootstrap resamples is used for assessment of measurement properties, direct relationships, mediation, explanation capacity, and prediction accuracy. In a simulated 420-case study, organizational learning capacity positively predicts digital adaptive capacity (β = 0.648***), digital adaptive capacity positively predicts resilience performance (β = 0.463***), and the indirect effect is equal to β = 0.300**. The model accounts for 62.4% of the variation in resilience performance. The results suggest that learning helps build resilience through quick adaptation of technologies, processes, and decision-making.

title: INTELLECTUAL CAPITAL AND CAPITAL STRUCTURE ON BUSINESS PERFORMANCE : THE MODERATING ROLE OF GOOD CORPORATE GOVERNANCE
summary: Food and beverage sub-sector companies in Indonesia face challenges in maintaining business performance amid increasing competition, rising production costs, and unstable economic conditions. Business performance measured using Return on Equity (ROE) experienced fluctuations and tended to decline during the 2021–2024 period. In addition, the effectiveness of intellectual capital management and capital structure policies is considered important in supporting company performance sustainability. Good Corporate Governance (GCG) is also believed to strengthen company management effectiveness and improve stakeholder trust. This study aims to analyze the effect of intellectual capital and capital structure on business performance with Good Corporate Governance as a moderating variable. This study uses a quantitative approach with associative research type. The data used are secondary data obtained from annual reports and financial statements of food and beverage sub-sector companies listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange during the 2021–2024 period. The sampling technique used purposive sampling. Data analysis was conducted using panel data regression and Moderated Regression Analysis (MRA) through EViews 10 software. The results show that intellectual capital and capital structure do not significantly affect business performance. Furthermore, Good Corporate Governance is unable to moderate the relationship between intellectual capital and business performance as well as the relationship between capital structure and business performance. These findings indicate that the implementation of intellectual capital management, capital structure policy, and corporate governance has not been fully effective in improving company performance. Companies are advised to optimize internal resource management, improve operational efficiency, maintain balanced financing policies, and strengthen the implementation of corporate governance to improve business performance sustainably.

title: Supply Chain Management Capabilities and Organizational Sustainability in Universities: Pandemic Preparedness Mixed Methods Evidence
summary: Background The coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic demonstrates the importance of organizational sustainability across all sectors, and universities are no exception. It revealed deep-seated fragilities in institutional supply chains, revealing that the ability to sustain core educational and research missions is inherently connected to the robustness of supply chain capabilities, thus underscoring the need to shift from a reactive to a proactive stance in university operations. This study examines the contribution of supply chain management capabilities and organizational sustainability among universities in Kenya in preparing for pandemics. Methods This study employed a mixed-method approach using a cross-sectional survey and Key Informant Interviews. Results This study provides robust empirical evidence that supply chain management capabilities are strongly and positively correlated with organizational sustainability in Kenyan universities, with correlation coefficients ranging from r = 0.772 among students to r = 0.838 among administrators. Regression analyses confirmed that supply chain capabilities significantly predicted sustainability outcomes, explaining between 60% and 73% of the variance, even after controlling for demographic factors, such as sex, age, institution type, and geographic region. This study developed a two-by-two typology to classify universities into four types with regard to supply chain capabilities and sustainability. Conclusions The results indicate that university administrators and policymakers must elevate supply chain development from an operational concern to a strategic priority, recognizing that well-designed systems render efficiency and sustainability mutually reinforcing rather than competing objectives.

title: Drone technology in medical supply chain management: A survey on enabling technologies, frameworks, and applications
summary: Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), or drones, have become known as a disruptive technology that can potentially enhance efficiency and accessibility in the medical supply chain by allowing the timely delivery of medical supplies such as vaccines, blood, organs and emergency drugs in remote and disaster-prone regions. This study provides a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of existing international research on the use of drones in medical supply chains, with a sample of 1,209 articles retrieved from the Dimensions.ai database for 2015-2026. VOSviewer was used to process the bibliographic information to determine publication growth and trends, leading authors and journals, country contributions and collaboration patterns, while a thematic analysis was conducted to identify the major and emerging research themes. The findings indicate that the past few years have witnessed a significant increase in the number of publications, which signifies increased interest in UAVs in healthcare supply chains, and that the most important research themes are emergency medical transportation, vaccine delivery, last-mile delivery of health care and drone system efficiency. In addition, a country-by-country examination reveals that the United States is at the forefront. Overall, the study provides information about recent trends and future perspectives on capitalizing on drone technology in medical supply chains.

title: ESG Pillar Composition and One-Year Accounting Loss Onset: Evidence from Bloomberg-Covered Firms, 2020–2024
summary: This study examines whether the internal composition of an environmental, social and governance (ESG) rating contains incremental information about one-year accounting-loss onset after the overall ESG level is held constant. Bloomberg environmental (E), social (S) and governance (G) pillar scores are reparameterised as ESGLevel = (E + S + G)/3, GovernanceHalo = G − (E + S)/2, and ESContrast = E − S. The FY2020–FY2024 panel contains 13,745 firm-years for 2751 relatively large listed firms; the principal model uses 8029 eligible transitions and 472 loss-onset events. A one-standard-deviation increase in GovernanceHalo has an average marginal effect of −0.02 percentage points (95% CI −0.87 to 0.83). Firm-blocked cross-validation provides essentially no incremental one-year predictive gain. Reviewer-driven sensitivity analyses using within-year standardised pillars, a firm fixed-effects linear probability model, Firth penalised logit, stabilised inverse-probability weighting for complete-case selection, and dynamic pre-trend controls do not reveal a stable loss-onset association. A separate 30% annual market-capitalisation contraction outcome is negatively associated with GovernanceHalo and remains significant after false-discovery-rate adjustment (q = 0.024), but it is a valuation-contraction proxy rather than an accounting-loss or crash-risk measure. The previously observed E/S score build-out is no longer evident after controls for prior score changes, current E/S level and historical score volatility. The evidence therefore rules out large average one-year loss-onset effects in this Bloomberg-covered sample while leaving open smaller, heterogeneous, longer-horizon and provider-specific effects.

title: Drivers of blockchain technology adoption in construction supply chains: a systematic literature review and scientometric synthesis
summary: Purpose Blockchain technology (BT) has attracted growing attention in construction supply chain management (CSCM), yet existing research predominantly emphasises applications, technical architectures and barriers, providing limited understanding of the pressures motivating adoption. This study, therefore, systematically identifies and synthesises the drivers of BT adoption in construction supply chains (CSCs). Design/methodology/approach A systematic literature review, conducted using the Scopus database, yielded 493 records. Following screening, 145 publications were retained for scientometric analysis, with 40 subsequently selected for qualitative content analysis. Findings The findings identify five interrelated driver themes: information governance; transactional and operational pressures; digital integration; sustainability and institutional pressures; and strategic and contextual pressures. Information fragmentation, limited visibility, trust and accountability deficits, coordination inefficiencies and unreliable provenance emerged as the most prominent motivations. However, driver salience varies across clients, contractors, subcontractors, suppliers, regulators and other supply-chain actors, demonstrating that adoption is a negotiated network-level decision rather than a uniform organisational response. Originality/value The findings provide a theoretically grounded basis for empirical research and help practitioners and policymakers align BT investments, governance arrangements and procurement interventions with clearly defined supply-chain problems rather than technology-led experimentation.

title: Saying ESG, Doing Less: Importance-Performance Gaps in Project Managers’ ESG Competencies Across Europe
summary: Environmental, social, and governance (ESG) integration in project management depends on the competencies of project managers, yet it remains unclear whether the gap between perceived importance and self-reported performance of these competencies is uniform across the three ESG dimensions or whether it is shaped by the maturity of organizational ESG integration. This study examines the magnitude, distribution, and contextual sensitivity of the importance–performance gap in ESG competencies. A structured survey measuring perceived importance and self-reported performance across 45 ESG competency items (15 per dimension) was administered to 754 project professionals from European countries. Paired-sample comparisons and effect sizes assessed gap magnitude; Kruskal–Wallis tests, a trend test, and pairwise comparisons assessed its variation by organizational ESG integration status; person-level correlations, benchmarked against the correlations of the importance and performance indices and adjusted for response style, examined whether dimension-specific gaps co-vary within individuals. A statistically significant positive gap was found for all 45 competencies (medium effect sizes, d = 0.51–0.54). Gap magnitude varied with organizational ESG integration status: it was largest, at 0.63–0.68 scale points, among professionals in organizations that had not yet integrated ESG and smallest, at 0.22 scale points, among those in organizations with one to three years of integration, with a partial rebound (0.24–0.34) beyond three years. Although the three dimensions cover distinct competency content, environmental, social, and governance gap scores correlated strongly within individuals (r = .77–.85), and remained high (r = .69–.79) after controlling for individual response style. The study documents person-level consistency in gap magnitude across the three ESG dimensions and interprets the patterns through institutional decoupling and value-action gap theory. ESG competency development should take account of organizational integration status and should address general enactment conditions alongside dimension-specific content.
